# Versioning

How a campaign's work is held in version control: the repositories it works in, their
branches and worktrees, how a batch lands its work and how each part is promoted. Where
things sit in the tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Repositories

A translation campaign produces a Rust codebase, so its repository is one: a new
repository created for the campaign, with the Rust at its root and the C it translates
inside it.

| campaign | repository | the C, under `c/` |
|---|---|---|
| wrap | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the source, pinned at the campaign's revision, which the campaign never changes |
| port | `<repo>-crustify` | a submodule of the campaign's fork of the source, `<repo>-fork`, on its `main` branch, which the modules' switches trim as they leave C |

`<repo>` is the source repository's name: a campaign on libgit2 is `libgit2-crustify`,
and a port's fork `libgit2-fork`. A wrap and a port campaign share the name, since wrapping a
codebase is a step towards replacing its implementation: a port continues a wrap campaign
in its repository. Both keep the C's history where it belongs, so that it can be read in the
submodule and an upstream release taken in by rebasing the fork's `main` onto it. The fork
mirrors the source's own `main` as `upstream/main`. The repositories are created under the
`crustify-rs` organization; the campaign's tree is [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s.

A library the target uses from outside its tree is wrapped in a wrap campaign of its own,
in `<source>-crustify`, named after the source it is built from, as
[`dependencies`](../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md) describes.

An audit reviews an existing Rust crate in its own repository, and creates none.

## 2. Branches

| branch | name | checked out |
|---|---|---|
| shipping | `main` in the campaign's own repository; `crustify/main` in an audit, beside the reviewed crate's own branches | never while the campaign runs |
| working | `crustify/devel` | in the repository's base dir |
| planner run | `crustify/planner/run-<n>` | in the repository's base dir, while its run is live |
| module | `crustify/modules/<link-unit>/<module>`, or `crustify/foundational/<link-unit>/<module>` for a foundational module | in its worktree, while it integrates |
| wave | `crustify/waves/wave-<index>` | never |
| batch | `crustify/batches/wave-<index>/batch-<index>` | in its worktree |

The shipping branch holds what the user has approved to ship: it advances only with the
user's approval, by a fast-forward to the working branch, and each advance is tagged on it,
`ship-<n>` numbered from 1, or `crustify/ship-<n>` in an audit. The working branch is where the
campaign integrates its work: planner runs fork from it and are promoted back to it, and
the modules are integrated into it, as `scheduling` describes.

A module's branch holds one run of its waves: its waves fork from
it and are promoted back to it, and it is integrated into the working branch once they
have landed, as [Integration](#45-integration) describes. `<module>` is the module's
`name`, the path of its TU or header below the C root; a path is never a directory of
another, so no two module branches collide.

A wave's branch is the integration branch its batches land on, a review wave's as much as
a translation wave's. It is never checked out: a landing push to a checked-out branch
fails, and one to a missing branch silently creates it.

An audit has no link units or modules: its waves are review waves, laid out the same
way.

## 3. Worktrees

Each batch has its own worktree, its `c/` a worktree of the base checkout's submodule, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/<batch id>`, named as
[`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md)'s Ids section names them, so that its name tells which
module it works on, and so does a module while it integrates, at
`crustify/.worktrees/<module dir>/integration`, beside its batches'. A
planner run has none: it runs in the repository's base dir, on its branch.

## 4. Landing

A batch lands its commits on the integration branch it was given, which is never checked
out. Before committing, the diff is checked to contain no unrelated work. A commit carries
no trailer but the co-author trailers of the campaign's [identity](#6-identity), and its
subject says what it does and which run made it. A batch's names its module's file and its
objective and ends with its run's id, as `refs.c: wrap 12 items (wave-3/batch-1/run-2)`,
and its body lists the items it translated by their anchors' paths, as
`fn::git_reference_lookup`, one per line; a review batch's two commits name what they file
and what they fix the same way, and a planner run's subject ends with its run's id. A
progress commit is `progress: wave-<index>`, and an integration's merge, in the campaign's
repository and on the fork's `main`, `integrate <module>`, the module written as
[`modules-schema`](../../artifacts/modules-schema/SKILL.md) writes it.

The landing operation is a local push of the batch's tip to the integration branch through
the repository's Git common directory, which accepts only a fast-forward. A direct ref
update is no substitute: its compare-and-swap form makes the update atomic, but does not
enforce that the new commit descends from the expected old commit.

### 4.1 The landing lock

An integration branch is landed on by one batch at a time, under its landing lock: an
exclusive `flock` on a file in the Git common directory, named after the branch with its
`refs/heads/` prefix dropped, so that every worktree of the repository sees the same lock:

```text
$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock
```

A batch whose validated work is committed on its own branch takes the lock and holds it
until its landing has succeeded:

1. it acquires the lock, waiting while another batch holds it;
2. it rebases only its own branch onto the current integration branch, once: nothing else
   lands while it holds the lock;
3. it resolves any conflict the rebase raises and runs again, on the rebased tree, the
   gates that could catch a regression of the integration, as
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes, fixing what fails;
4. it pushes the fast-forward, which nothing can reject; and
5. it releases the lock.

A conflict or a failing gate is resolved under the lock rather than after releasing it, so
that the branch cannot move again in between and no batch rebases twice.

The waiter blocks in `flock` itself, so the kernel wakes it the moment the lock is released,
and nothing polls. Once it holds the lock, it hands the locked descriptor to a process of
its own, detached from the shell that started it and bound to the lifetime of the agent's
CLI: a `flock` lock belongs to the open file, so that process keeps it after the command
that took it exits, until that CLI ends, however it ends, and the kernel releases it. The
holder records itself beside the lock, in `<integration branch>.lock.holder`, as its own pid
and the CLI's. A waiter bounds each wait, to stay within the time a single command may run,
and waits again when it expires. For example, with `$CLI_PID` the agent CLI's pid, found by
walking up the shell's parent processes:
<!-- TODO: this procedure must run exactly so: it belongs in a script beside this skill,
documented by its `--help`, as `authoring` describes. -->

```bash
lock="$(git rev-parse --git-common-dir)/crustify/landing/<integration branch>.lock"
mkdir -p "$(dirname "$lock")"
# wait in the kernel, up to 10 minutes per command; then hand the lock to a detached holder
sh -c '
  exec 9>"$1"
  flock -w 600 9 || exit 1
  setsid sh -c "echo \"\$\$ $2\" > \"$1.holder\"; exec tail --pid=$2 -f /dev/null" 9>&9 &
' sh "$lock" "$CLI_PID"
# release, once the push has succeeded
holder=$(cut -d' ' -f1 "$lock.holder"); rm -f "$lock.holder"; kill "$holder"
```

The holder file is removed before the holder is ended, while the lock is still held, so
that a release never removes the next holder's record.

The lock has no timeout: the regression gates it covers vary in length. A holder that has
stopped making progress keeps it until its agent is ended. That releases it where the
agent ran in a CLI of its own. An agent that shared its CLI with others leaves its holder
running: the holder is then ended as a release ends it, by the pid its record names, the
record removed first. The batch is then run again, as any failed batch is.

### 4.2 Commits

Every landing is a fast-forward, so an integration branch is linear, and each batch's
commits are one unbroken run of it, ending at its branch's tip and starting after the wave
base or the tip of the batch that landed before it: the commits its branch reaches and
neither the wave base nor the wave's other landed batches reach, oldest first, which
become the batch's `commits` in `schedule.json`.

The integration branch is never reset, force-updated or moved backward, and nothing is
pushed to a remote. The worktree stays after landing, until it is purged as [Lifecycle](#5-lifecycle)
describes.
<!-- TODO: when the working and shipping branches, and a wrapper's, are pushed to their
remotes is not specified yet, though a wrapper's reuse and a Git-pinned dependency need
it. -->

### 4.3 Promotion

A wave that has landed every batch is promoted to the branch it forked from, the module's
branch or the working branch, by a fast-forward to its tip, with the same local push
through the Git common directory, which rejects anything but a fast-forward.

### 4.4 Progress

The progress recorded while waves run, in `schedule.json`, the dashboard's usage and
campaign cells, and the `status` of a module in `modules.json` that a wrap batch ahead of
its consumer freezes, is committed on the working branch whenever no module is integrating. No agent writes
`schedule.json`, and no module branch changes it.

### 4.5 Integration

A module's branch is integrated into the working branch once the
last wave of its run has been promoted to it. Other modules may have been integrated since
it forked, so the working branch is merged into it, in its worktree, rather than the
other way around: the module's commits keep their ids, which its batches' `commits`
record, and the working branch still moves only by fast-forward.

1. The working branch's tip is merged into the module's branch. The files every module
   adds to, the dashboard's rows, the raw bindings' allowlists, `src/lib.rs`'s module
   declarations and the safe crate's export features, conflict additively, and so does a
   module's file in which two runs homed different items ahead of their consumers, with
   the declarations of the modules on its path: each conflict
   keeps both sides, a file's items in one of each of its regions, and the generated bindings are regenerated from the merged input. Any other conflict is a defect of the integration, resolved without
   discarding either side. No merge is committed while its tree holds a conflict marker,
   here or wherever a branch takes another by merge, such as a wave's branch taking the
   working branch, so that every branch forked from it starts from a tree that builds.
2. The merge's tree passes the gates of
   [`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section, and in
   a port campaign, in the run that holds the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port`
   items, the module's switch from C to Rust, which happens once, as
   [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes:
   its export feature is deleted, and the C test cases none of its `unit_pub` tests carries
   over are listed before its C tests leave.
3. The working branch is fast-forwarded to the module's branch.

Modules integrate one at a time, and nothing else is committed on the working branch while
one does, so that its fast-forward cannot be rejected. A port's later-stage waves come after
their module's switch, are promoted to the working branch, and integrate nothing, as
the porting workflow's Later stages section describes.

## 5. Lifecycle

Each branch and worktree exists only while its part of the campaign needs it. Before a part starts, everything it is named for exists; once it is promoted, what
only it needed is purged.

### 5.1 Campaign

The working branch is created during setup, in the repository the campaign creates, with
the C under `c/` and `crustify/CRUSTIFY.md` in its first commit. The shipping branch is created at the same commit and stays there
until the user first approves shipping. Both last for the campaign.

The working branch is committed to only when nothing is being promoted or integrated to
it, so that every promotion and integration is a fast-forward: the progress recorded in
the meantime stays in the base checkout's working tree until then, as
[Progress](#44-progress) describes.

### 5.2 Planner runs

A planner run's branch is forked from the working branch's tip and checked out in the repository's base dir. Once the run has committed, the working
branch is checked out and fast-forwarded to it, and the next run forks from there.

### 5.3 Modules

A module's base is the working branch's commit that holds its scaffolded `.rs` file and
the settings it runs under, committed before its first wave.

A module's branch is forked from its base before its first wave,
once the waves of other modules that its waves depend on have been integrated. A module
whose waves the order splits, such as one that wraps a cut dependency ahead of its
consumer, or one whose wave waits for an item another module's run holds, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Wrap batches section describes, runs once per contiguous run of its waves, each run on a branch forked anew
from the working branch. In a port campaign, only the run that holds the last wave of the
module's `wrap` and `port` items switches it from C; an earlier run's integration merges
its Rust alone, the module still C. Once a run has been integrated, its branch and worktree
are purged; its end state is the working branch's commit its last run integrates into.

### 5.4 Waves

A wave's integration branch is forked from its module's branch's tip, or, for a port's
later-stage wave, which runs after its module's switch, from the working branch's tip,
before any of its batches launch, so that it exists before the first landing, as [Branches](#2-branches)
requires; that commit is the wave's base.
Once every batch has landed, the wave is promoted, as [Promotion](#43-promotion)
describes, and its branch purged.

A translation wave's review batches are batches of the wave itself, and it is promoted once
they have landed too. An audit's review waves fork as any wave does.

### 5.5 Batches

A batch's branch and worktree, forked from its wave branch's tip, are created before it
launches, with its run dir, as [`layout`](../layout/SKILL.md) describes. The gitignored state its tree needs and does
not build itself, such as shared analysis databases, is symlinked from the base checkout,
and its `c/` is a worktree of the base checkout's submodule at the commit the superproject
records.
Once the batch has landed, its worktree is purged; its branch stays until its commits are
recorded in `schedule.json`, since they are derived from it, as
[Landing](#4-landing) describes. A batch that fails keeps its branch and worktree for
inspection; they are removed before it is run again, which forks them anew.

## 6. Identity

Every commit of a campaign, in its repository and its wrappers', is authored and committed
as Crustify, whose GitHub account is `crustify-ai` and whose git identity is
`crustify <crustify@berkeley.edu>`, whatever the repository's git configuration says,
unless the settings' `identity` answer names another: an author and any co-authors, each
as `Name <email>`. The author named there then authors and commits every commit, and each
message ends with one `Co-Authored-By:` trailer per co-author and no other, none that an
agent's host suggests included.

The identity is passed explicitly, as configuration on the command line, to every command
that writes a commit, a rebase, a merge and a cherry-pick as much as a commit, since the
host may have no git identity of its own.
---
name: task-schema
description: "The fields of a run's task.json: run fields, batch fields, routes and items. Read before writing or reading a task.json."
---

# task.json schema

Field meaning for `task.json`, the one input of a run, in its run dir: of a `wrap` batch,
a `port` batch or a later stage's, a review batch, or a planner run. One task is one run's
entire worklist and how it runs.

A translation batch's task is one batch entry of `schedule-schema`,
packed from its wave's items when the wave starts. When the batch launches, that entry is
written as `task.json`: its `kind` as `objective`, its `items`, the
[batch fields](#2-batch-fields) that place it in the schedule, and the
[run fields](#1-run-fields).

`task.json` sits in its run's dir, as [`layout`](../../operations/layout/SKILL.md)'s Artifact dirs section spells it.
Its `session_id` is recorded in it as soon as the run's session has one, which ties the run
to its transcript and its records in crustify's home; a task that already holds one is not
run again. A batch that is run again gets a new run dir and task, so every attempt keeps
its own.

```json
{
  "objective": "wrap",
  "wave": 0,
  "batch": 0,
  "link_unit": "libavutil",
  "module": "libavutil/frame.c",
  "foundational": false,
  "base_branch": "crustify/waves/wave-0",
  "backend": "claude",
  "billing": "subscription",
  "revisions": {"crustify": "<sha>", "wavefront": "<sha>", "ffimap": "<sha>", "ffibox": "<sha>"},
  "items": [
    {
      "name": "AVFrame",
      "defined_in": "libavutil/frame.h",
      "kind": "struct",
      "field_users": ["data", "linesize"],
      "typedefs": [],
      "home": "src/libavutil/libavutil/frame.rs"
    }
  ]
}
```

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `objective` | execution objective for every item: `wrap` or `port`, or a later stage of a port campaign, `port/layout`, `port/memory` or `port/unexport`, as `scheduling`'s Later stages section describes |
| `items` | non-empty worklist; every item selects the same route |
| `wave`, `batch`, `link_unit`, `module`, `foundational` | the [batch fields](#2-batch-fields) |
| `base_branch`, `backend`, `billing`, `model_proxy`, `session_id`, `args`, `revisions` | the [run fields](#1-run-fields) |

All but `model_proxy`, `session_id` and `args` are required, and no other root
field is accepted. `session_id` is absent until the run starts.

## 1. Run fields

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `base_branch` | the unchecked-out integration branch the agent lands on: its wave branch, or in an audit its review wave branch; a `refs/heads/` prefix is accepted |
| `backend` | the provider CLI the agent runs on: `claude`, Claude Code, or `codex` |
| `billing` | how the provider CLI authenticates: `subscription`, its own logged-in account, or `api`, an API key from the environment |
| `model_proxy` | optional: the gateway the CLI's requests go through, with its own key, such as `openrouter`; it needs `api` billing, and its rates price the run |
| `session_id` | the session the run became, recorded once it starts, never before |
| `revisions` | the commits of Crustify and of each tool the run uses, by name, such as `{"crustify": "<sha>", "wavefront": "<sha>"}`, recorded as it launches, from the checkouts it reads and runs |
| `args` | optional: arguments passed to the provider CLI unchanged, after Crustify's own, in the CLI's own syntax, such as `["--model", "opus", "--effort", "high"]` |

Without `args` naming one, the CLI runs its own default model; Codex through a model proxy
needs its model named, as the proxy knows it. A batch's task carries `base_branch`,
`backend` and `billing`. A planner task carries `backend` and `billing` only: a planner
run commits on the planner branch it is spawned on, which is then promoted to the working
branch, `crustify/devel`.

## 2. Batch fields

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `wave` | the `index` of the batch's wave in `schedule.json` |
| `batch` | the batch's `index` within that wave |
| `link_unit` | its wave's `link_unit`; `null` in an audit, which has no decomposition |
| `module` | its wave's `module`, the module's `name`; `null` in an audit |
| `foundational` | its wave's `foundational` |

`wave` and `batch` form the batch id, `wave-<wave>/batch-<batch>`, which names the batch's
branch, worktree and reviews dir as `versioning` and `layout` spell them, and leads from the run
back to the batch's entry in `schedule.json`. A batch's task carries all five; a planner
task carries none.

## 3. Task message

An agent's task message names what its Inputs section lists, its `task.json` among them,
and the instructions its run needs beyond its role, if any, which take precedence over
the rest of its prompt where the two conflict. It is kept in the run's artifact dir, as
`task.md` beside `task.json`, so that git records what the agent was told along with the
task.

## 4. Review batches

A review batch carries, instead of `objective`, an optional `objectives` array, and a Rust
worklist instead of `items`: in a translate campaign, the commits its translation batches
landed; in an audit, modules of the crate, commits of its history or reports to revisit, as
[`audit-workflow`](../../workflows/audit-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Worksets section gives them.

```json
{
  "objectives": ["lifecycle", "unsafety", "ub", "equiv", "fix"],
  "commits": ["3f2a9c1", "8be04d7"],
  "wave": 1,
  "batch": 0,
  "link_unit": "libavutil",
  "module": "libavutil/frame.c",
  "foundational": false,
  "base_branch": "crustify/waves/wave-1",
  "backend": "claude",
  "billing": "subscription",
  "revisions": {"crustify": "<sha>", "wavefront": "<sha>", "ffimap": "<sha>", "ffibox": "<sha>"}
}
```

```json
{
  "objectives": ["ub", "contracts", "disclose"],
  "paths": ["src/frame.rs", {"path": "src/codec.rs", "types": ["Decoder"], "trait_impls": ["Drop for Decoder"], "functions": ["open_input"]}]
}
```

```json
{"objectives": ["revisit", "disclose", "fix"], "reports": ["crustify/reviews/<module dir>/<batch id>/ub_safe/<slug>"]}
```

```json
{"objectives": ["ub", "contracts", "logic"], "paths": ["src", "tests"], "module_pass": true, "wave_gates": true}
```

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `objectives` | the review objectives to run; optional, every one that applies when absent |
| `commits` | distinct commit ids, as they sit on its wave's branch; route `commits`: the `commits` of the batches its schedule entry `reviews`, whose `items` there list the C items they bound or ported, or, in an audit, commits of the crate's own history |
| `paths` | repo-relative source files and directories; route `paths`. An entry may instead be `{"path", "types", "trait_impls", "functions"}`, naming the parts of a module too large to review whole: types, each with its fields and inherent impls; trait impls, each `<trait> for <type>` as its impl header spells it; and free functions |
| `reports` | repo-relative report dirs, `<reviews dir>/<kind>/<slug>`, to revisit |
| `wave_gates` | optional, `false` when absent: `true` on the wave's last review batch, launched once every translation batch of the wave has landed, which runs the wave's gates, as `reviewing`'s Gates section describes; only on a batch with `commits`, or on a module pass; in an audit, only on the crate pass |
| `module_pass` | optional, `false` when absent: `true` on a module pass, whose `paths` are its module's Rust file and its test files in each suite, or, on an audit's crate pass, the crate's source and test roots, and which carries `wave_gates` |

The batch and run fields are required, as on a translation task; the examples after the
first leave them out, and the last is an audit's crate pass. An audit's batch has a `null` `link_unit` and `module`, and a `false`
`foundational`.
A batch carries `commits` or `paths`, not both, and needs one of them or `reports`; one
with only `reports` has route `reports`. A module path appears once, and a module object
names one or more of `types`, `trait_impls` and `functions`, each a distinct list. `reports` is given exactly when `revisit` is among the
objectives, and an absent `objectives` includes `revisit` exactly when `reports` is given.
The optional `wave_gates` and `module_pass` are the only other root fields accepted.

The objectives are those `reviewing`'s Objectives section describes and those the
installed tools' skills add. A batch naming an objective
neither offers is rejected.

## 5. Planner tasks

A planner task says only how a planner run runs. What it plans is the branch it is spawned
on, forked from the working branch: every run emits what the committed plan lacks, updates what follows an earlier
schema, corrects what earlier runs decided, and re-plans the waves its changes move.

```json
{"backend": "claude", "billing": "subscription", "revisions": {"crustify": "<sha>", "wavefront": "<sha>"}}
```

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `backend`, `billing`, `model_proxy`, `session_id`, `args`, `revisions` | the [run fields](#1-run-fields) |

`backend`, `billing` and `revisions` are required, and no other root field is accepted. It is written as
`task.json` in the run's artifact dir, `crustify/artifacts/planner/run-<n>/`.

## 6. items[*]

Every field is required on every item, and no other field is accepted.

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | C entity name, non-empty: a function pointer written inline is named by its signature |
| `defined_in` | path of its definition below the C root |
| `kind` | what the C entity is: `struct`, `union`, `enum`, `function`, `global`, `macro`, `function_pointer`, declared by a typedef or written inline, or `typedef`, one that names no struct, union, enum or function pointer |
| `field_users` | the members of a struct, a union or an enum its consumers use: a struct's or a union's fields, whose accessors the batch writes, or an enum's constants; empty on any other kind |
| `typedefs` | the typedefs that name a struct, a union, an enum or a function pointer besides its `name`, which the batch binds with it; empty on any other kind |
| `home` | `.rs` path, relative to the repository's root, the item is authored into |

`(name, defined_in)` identifies an item and must be unique within the batch. A
`port/layout` batch holds only structs, unions and enums, a `port/memory` batch only
structs and unions, and a `port/unexport` batch only functions, globals and function
pointers.
`field_users` and `typedefs` must not repeat a name.

`home` is the sole placement input: no other artifact decides where an item goes, so the
Rust tree a wave's batches name is not restructured while the wave runs.

## 7. Routes

`kind` selects the agent route, and every item in a batch must select the same one. A
batch mixing routes is rejected.

| kind | route |
|---|---|
| `struct`, `union`, `enum`, `typedef`, and a `macro` that generates types | `type` |
| `function`, `global`, `function_pointer`, and any other `macro` | `symbol` |

A macro generates types when its record in the planning tools lists the instance types it
mints: its instances share the one generic the type route writes for it, as
[`binding-symbols`](../../rust/binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section describes.

A batch of a foundational module routes like any other. Its `module` and `foundational`
name the module, which `modules.json` marks `foundational`, and its items with a lifecycle
role are bound as strategies (`binding-symbols`, Lifecycle strategies).

## 8. Evolution reviews

An evolution review's task names the change it reviews, as
[`evolution`](../../crustify/evolution/SKILL.md)'s Review section describes:

```json
{"backend": "claude", "billing": "subscription", "args": ["--model", "opus"],
 "revisions": {"crustify": "<working branch sha>", "wavefront": "<working branch sha>"},
 "component": "wavefront", "branch": "<campaign-id>/evolution/<slug>", "commit": "<sha>",
 "proposal": "crustify/evolution/<slug>"}
```

| root field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `backend`, `billing`, `model_proxy`, `session_id`, `args`, `revisions` | the [run fields](#1-run-fields) |
| `component` | the component the change is made in: `crustify`, or a tool by name |
| `branch` | the evolution branch that holds the change, in the component's repository |
| `commit` | the commit of `branch` the review reviews, the only one its verdict lets land |
| `proposal` | the proposal's dir in the campaign's repository |

All but `model_proxy`, `session_id` and `args` are required, and no other root field is
accepted. Its `revisions` are those of the campaign's working branches the review runs under,
never the change's. It is written as `task.json` in the run's artifact dir,
`crustify/artifacts/evolution/<slug>/review-<n>/`.

---
name: analysis
description: "How a scheduled C item is analysed before it is bound or ported: what is inspected, what the analysis establishes and how its findings shape the Rust. Read before binding or porting any item, and when reviewing either."
---

# Item analysis

How a scheduled C item is analysed before it is bound or ported. The analysis is the same
for both: what it establishes shapes the binding or port that follows.

## 1. Scope

Each item is analysed from its source declarations and definitions, its dependency closure,
its callers, its field touchers and its existing Rust consumers. For every pointer field,
argument and return, every code path that stores, transfers, clones, retains or frees it is
inspected.

## 2. Findings

The analysis establishes:

- ownership and transfer direction;
- shared or mutable access;
- nullability;
- scalar, array, or other cardinality;
- type erasure and known element types;
- borrow and keepalive relationships;
- address retention: whether C keeps an object's address beyond the call that receives it,
  to read it, call back with it or free it;
- construction, clone, and destruction paths;
- states and transitions: the states each type's objects pass through, and the calls that
  move them between states, in the orders C allows, with the calls a callback may make on
  the object its caller lends it, and those that would corrupt the caller's state;
- out-parameters: the pointer arguments a function only writes through;
- string encodings, where a string is known to hold text or a path; and
- failure reporting: the status or sentinel returns and the error state beside the call
  through which a function fails, and the outcomes its callers treat as ordinary.

Observed behaviour overrides names and comments. A distinction the analysis establishes is
preserved in Rust rather than flattened into a copy of an ambiguous C signature.
---
name: porting
description: "How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust: its native API, its later stages, the FFI boundary and its exports, and the routes porting-types and porting-symbols give types and symbols. Read before porting any item, and when reviewing ports."
---

# Porting

How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust. A port starts from the item's
analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes, and keeps C interoperability
and observable behaviour for as long as C consumes the item. A type takes the type route,
for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`porting-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a
symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, static inline functions
and macros, as [`porting-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

A port gives an item its native safe API at once, and that API does not change after it.
An item the remaining C still uses keeps a C form behind it, its C layout, its storage in
C's allocator, its export or its integer values, so that the C keeps working while its
Rust consumers stay agnostic of which form implements it. The later stages its kind
describes below migrate that form to Rust, part by part, once the switches that free
it have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section schedules them. An item no C uses is native in its API and its implementation from
its port.

A later stage changes the item and the code inside the crate that reaches its C form, in
its module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions
section describes, never the safe API its consumers use, and keeps the item's tests
passing. A stage that moves state out of C, a lock or a handle a type held in its C layout,
or memory C's allocator held, moves its uses onto the standard library where
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section lets it.

## 1. FFI boundary

`binding`'s Safe boundary section applies to a port unchanged. When a wrapper of the item
already exists, because a module that ran before needed it, the port keeps that wrapper's
safe API and replaces only what is behind it, so that its consumers do not change, as do
its later stages. A standard-library operation is used directly when it is equivalent and
no C-interoperability requirement remains, an out-of-tree library's entity included, as
`binding`'s Safe boundary section describes.

While C consumers remain, a ported item is re-exported to C as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes:

- The raw gateway, its module's `ffi_export` region, reconstructs safe wrappers and calls
  the native function.
- The gateway is compiled only under its module's export feature, which stays off until
  the module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they replace.
- At the switch, the Rust static library is linked in place of the TU through the actual
  build system, without assuming link mechanics, and the TU is deleted, as
  [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes.
---
name: porting-symbols
description: "How a scheduled C symbol is reimplemented in safe Rust, porting's symbol route: functions and their exports, globals, function pointers, static inline functions and macros, each with its later stages. Read before porting any symbol, and when reviewing ports."
---

# Porting symbols

How a scheduled C symbol is reimplemented in safe Rust: the symbol route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s; the types it reaches are
[`porting-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s.

A ported symbol's implementation is translated to safe, idiomatic Rust with its observable
behaviour preserved.

## 1. Functions

A ported function takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Functions
section gives a function, or keeps its wrapper's, as [`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes.

A function no wrapper gives an API yet, whose body only reads or writes one member, or only
returns a value an existing item of its own module's safe API already gives, is ported as
that item, so that the port writes no second API: the accessor or method carries the
function's `Replaces` anchor and alias beside its own. Its export, where remaining C calls
it, is written in the module's gateway, over that item.

A function that remaining C calls or takes the address of is exported, as
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes. Its gateway undoes what the safe API converted,
so that its C callers see what the C function did: it rebuilds the safe arguments from the
C ones, writes the out-parameters and buffers through the pointers C passed, and reports a
failure through the function's C error convention, its return and the error state the C
function set, `errno` included, which the Rust behind it never sets. A panic is caught at
the gateway and reported as a failure, or aborts where the function cannot fail: none
unwinds into C. The gateway checks each export against the raw binding of the C declaration
it replaces, as [`testing-gates`](../../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions
section asks, in a constant the compiler evaluates, `const _: () = { let _ = [sys::<name>,
<name>]; };`, whose two function items coerce to one function-pointer type only where their
signatures agree; the binding is allowlisted for it where the bindings lack it. A variadic function's export cannot be defined on stable Rust, so a shim
keeps its C signature, as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, and calls
a fixed-arity export with the arguments it formats or unpacks. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the
export, with the raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it and its declaration in its
header, once no remaining C references it. C that only a configuration the target is built
without compiles, such as another platform's, is no remaining C: like a test case
configured out, as [`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Tests
follow their modules section describes, it holds no export back, and a build under that
configuration meets the function undeclared where it calls it.

A lifecycle routine's port reimplements it behind the policy its type's port or wrap
wrote, which it repoints at the Rust routine, and writes no API of its own, as `binding-types`'
Lifecycle section has the symbol route skip what a type batch emitted. The last of its
type's own module's memory users to be ported moves its storage to Rust's allocator,
unless C of other modules still allocates or frees it raw, which leaves that move to its
`port/memory`.

## 2. Globals

A ported global takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Globals section gives a global, or keeps its wrapper's. Rust holds its storage from its
port, beside its module's C, which keeps its own copy until the switch; from then on
the Rust's is the only one. A global that remaining C accesses
is exported, as a function is, and keeps the C layout and the synchronization protocol
those accesses rely on while it is. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the export, as
a function's does, and its storage then takes a native form, as state moved out of C does.
A thread-local one cannot be defined for C on stable Rust, so a shim keeps its C definition,
as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, until that stage. A global no
remaining C accesses is native from its port.

## 3. Function pointers

A ported function pointer keeps the safe callable type
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section gives it, which is its API from its port: its Rust consumers, and
the ported code that calls it, use that type alone. While remaining C calls a function
pointer of its type or supplies one, its C form stays beneath it: the function-pointer type
of its raw binding, the trampolines through which a Rust closure reaches the C that calls
it, and the `unsafe` constructor through which a C function reaches Rust, passed to an
export, whose gateway builds the C variant from the function and the context it receives,
or stored where C wrote it. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes that C form, with the
raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it, once no remaining C references it, as
[`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section times it. A
function pointer no remaining C calls or supplies by its port is native in its
implementation too: its closure or trait alone.
A function pointer on the target's public API keeps its closure or trait through its
`port/unexport`, even when Rust alone implements it, so that the deferred public C API, as
[`conventions`](../../conventions/SKILL.md)'s Exports section describes, can let C
implement it again.

## 4. Static inline functions

A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.
<!-- TODO: cross-language LTO (`-Clinker-plugin-lto`, with a clang whose LLVM matches
rustc's) would inline the export back into its C callers. -->

## 5. Macros

A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,
which reaches the Rust items its expansion uses once they are ported. A macro a TU defines
goes with its TU. A macro a header defines, internal or public API that another module's C
may expand, also stays in its header for the remaining C, unexported, and its C and Rust
forms are not linked, beyond the Rust form's annotation. It keeps expanding where remaining C
invokes it, until its header goes with the last C file that includes it, as
[`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Principles section
describes: a type generator keeps minting the instances its remaining invocations define,
and what an expansion calls or accesses is reached as any remaining C reaches it, a
function or global Rust owns through its export, a type through its C layout. An
expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration is ported once where every
configuration's expansion computes the same result for every input, and its documentation

# Item analysis

How a scheduled C item is analysed before it is bound or ported. The analysis is the same
for both: what it establishes shapes the binding or port that follows.

## 1. Scope

Each item is analysed from its source declarations and definitions, its dependency closure,
its callers, its field touchers and its existing Rust consumers. For every pointer field,
argument and return, every code path that stores, transfers, clones, retains or frees it is
inspected.

## 2. Findings

The analysis establishes:

- ownership and transfer direction;
- shared or mutable access;
- nullability;
- scalar, array, or other cardinality;
- type erasure and known element types;
- borrow and keepalive relationships;
- address retention: whether C keeps an object's address beyond the call that receives it,
  to read it, call back with it or free it;
- construction, clone, and destruction paths;
- states and transitions: the states each type's objects pass through, and the calls that
  move them between states, in the orders C allows, with the calls a callback may make on
  the object its caller lends it, and those that would corrupt the caller's state;
- out-parameters: the pointer arguments a function only writes through;
- string encodings, where a string is known to hold text or a path; and
- failure reporting: the status or sentinel returns and the error state beside the call
  through which a function fails, and the outcomes its callers treat as ordinary.

Observed behaviour overrides names and comments. A distinction the analysis establishes is
preserved in Rust rather than flattened into a copy of an ambiguous C signature.

description: "How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust: its native API, its later stages, the FFI boundary and its exports, and the routes porting-types and porting-symbols give types and symbols. Read before porting any item, and when reviewing ports."

# Porting

How a scheduled C item is reimplemented in safe Rust. A port starts from the item's
analysis, as [`analysis`](../analysis/SKILL.md) describes, and keeps C interoperability
and observable behaviour for as long as C consumes the item. A type takes the type route,
for structs, unions, enums and typedefs, as [`porting-types`](types/SKILL.md) describes; a
symbol the symbol route, for functions, globals, function pointers, static inline functions
and macros, as [`porting-symbols`](symbols/SKILL.md) describes.

A port gives an item its native safe API at once, and that API does not change after it.
An item the remaining C still uses keeps a C form behind it, its C layout, its storage in
C's allocator, its export or its integer values, so that the C keeps working while its
Rust consumers stay agnostic of which form implements it. The later stages its kind
describes below migrate that form to Rust, part by part, once the switches that free
it have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section schedules them. An item no C uses is native in its API and its implementation from
its port.

A later stage changes the item and the code inside the crate that reaches its C form, in
its module's unsafe regions, as the [conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Unsafe regions
section describes, never the safe API its consumers use, and keeps the item's tests
passing. A stage that moves state out of C, a lock or a handle a type held in its C layout,
or memory C's allocator held, moves its uses onto the standard library where
[`binding`](../binding/SKILL.md)'s Safe boundary section lets it.

## 1. FFI boundary

`binding`'s Safe boundary section applies to a port unchanged. When a wrapper of the item
already exists, because a module that ran before needed it, the port keeps that wrapper's
safe API and replaces only what is behind it, so that its consumers do not change, as do
its later stages. A standard-library operation is used directly when it is equivalent and
no C-interoperability requirement remains, an out-of-tree library's entity included, as
`binding`'s Safe boundary section describes.

While C consumers remain, a ported item is re-exported to C as the
[conventions](../conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes:

- The raw gateway, its module's `ffi_export` region, reconstructs safe wrappers and calls
  the native function.
- The gateway is compiled only under its module's export feature, which stays off until
  the module switches, so that the exports never collide with the C they replace.
- At the switch, the Rust static library is linked in place of the TU through the actual
  build system, without assuming link mechanics, and the TU is deleted, as
  [`porting-workflow`](../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Builds section describes.

# Porting symbols

How a scheduled C symbol is reimplemented in safe Rust: the symbol route, which follows
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section and starts from
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s; the types it reaches are
[`porting-types`](../types/SKILL.md)'s.

A ported symbol's implementation is translated to safe, idiomatic Rust with its observable
behaviour preserved.

## 1. Functions

A ported function takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Functions
section gives a function, or keeps its wrapper's, as [`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes.

A function no wrapper gives an API yet, whose body only reads or writes one member, or only
returns a value an existing item of its own module's safe API already gives, is ported as
that item, so that the port writes no second API: the accessor or method carries the
function's `Replaces` anchor and alias beside its own. Its export, where remaining C calls
it, is written in the module's gateway, over that item.

A function that remaining C calls or takes the address of is exported, as
[`porting`](../SKILL.md)'s FFI boundary section describes. Its gateway undoes what the safe API converted,
so that its C callers see what the C function did: it rebuilds the safe arguments from the
C ones, writes the out-parameters and buffers through the pointers C passed, and reports a
failure through the function's C error convention, its return and the error state the C
function set, `errno` included, which the Rust behind it never sets. A panic is caught at
the gateway and reported as a failure, or aborts where the function cannot fail: none
unwinds into C. The gateway checks each export against the raw binding of the C declaration
it replaces, as [`testing-gates`](../../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)' Regressions
section asks, in a constant the compiler evaluates, `const _: () = { let _ = [sys::<name>,
<name>]; };`, whose two function items coerce to one function-pointer type only where their
signatures agree; the binding is allowlisted for it where the bindings lack it. A variadic function's export cannot be defined on stable Rust, so a shim
keeps its C signature, as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, and calls
a fixed-arity export with the arguments it formats or unpacks. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the
export, with the raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it and its declaration in its
header, once no remaining C references it. C that only a configuration the target is built
without compiles, such as another platform's, is no remaining C: like a test case
configured out, as [`porting-workflow`](../../../workflows/porting-workflow/SKILL.md)'s Tests
follow their modules section describes, it holds no export back, and a build under that
configuration meets the function undeclared where it calls it.

A lifecycle routine's port reimplements it behind the policy its type's port or wrap
wrote, which it repoints at the Rust routine, and writes no API of its own, as `binding-types`'
Lifecycle section has the symbol route skip what a type batch emitted. The last of its
type's own module's memory users to be ported moves its storage to Rust's allocator,
unless C of other modules still allocates or frees it raw, which leaves that move to its
`port/memory`.

## 2. Globals

A ported global takes the safe API [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s
Globals section gives a global, or keeps its wrapper's. Rust holds its storage from its
port, beside its module's C, which keeps its own copy until the switch; from then on
the Rust's is the only one. A global that remaining C accesses
is exported, as a function is, and keeps the C layout and the synchronization protocol
those accesses rely on while it is. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes the export, as
a function's does, and its storage then takes a native form, as state moved out of C does.
A thread-local one cannot be defined for C on stable Rust, so a shim keeps its C definition,
as [`bindgen`](../../bindgen/SKILL.md)'s shims are compiled, until that stage. A global no
remaining C accesses is native from its port.

## 3. Function pointers

A ported function pointer keeps the safe callable type
[`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Function pointers section gives it, which is its API from its port: its Rust consumers, and
the ported code that calls it, use that type alone. While remaining C calls a function
pointer of its type or supplies one, its C form stays beneath it: the function-pointer type
of its raw binding, the trampolines through which a Rust closure reaches the C that calls
it, and the `unsafe` constructor through which a C function reaches Rust, passed to an
export, whose gateway builds the C variant from the function and the context it receives,
or stored where C wrote it. Its later stage, `port/unexport`, removes that C form, with the
raw binding and the allowlist entry that reach it, once no remaining C references it, as
[`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section times it. A
function pointer no remaining C calls or supplies by its port is native in its
implementation too: its closure or trait alone.
A function pointer on the target's public API keeps its closure or trait through its
`port/unexport`, even when Rust alone implements it, so that the deferred public C API, as
[`conventions`](../../conventions/SKILL.md)'s Exports section describes, can let C
implement it again.

## 4. Static inline functions

A `static inline` function a header defines is internal API of the module the
decomposition gives it, and is ported as its other functions are. Its C callers expand its
body in their own TUs, so an export alone does not reach them: at the module's
switch, the header's definition is replaced by its prototype, and the remaining C
calls the Rust module's export, under the function's bare name, where it inlined the body.

rustc's) would inline the export back into its C callers. -->

## 5. Macros

A macro takes the Rust form [`binding-symbols`](../../binding/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Macros section gives it,

describes: a type generator keeps minting the instances its remaining invocations define,
and what an expansion calls or accesses is reached as any remaining C reaches it, a
function or global Rust owns through its export, a type through its C layout. An
expansion site is a use by the function that holds it, so it holds back the later stages
of what it reaches, as [`scheduling`](../../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section counts its users.

A macro whose expansion depends on the build's configuration is ported once where every
configuration's expansion computes the same result for every input, and its documentation
names the branches the build does not take. Only one whose branches differ in what they
compute keeps the shim `binding-symbols` gives it: a port reimplements the body, and a shim
over the C's expansion would make it a binding. A symbol alias of an out-of-tree library's
entity is ported as that entity's route reaches it, as
[`dependencies`](../../../planning/dependencies/SKILL.md)'s Confirmation section checks it:
through the standard library, it is a native function.

# Porting workflow

How a `port` campaign proceeds. It follows the [binding workflow](../binding-workflow/SKILL.md) throughout;
this document gives the principles a port follows and where it differs. How each item is
ported is [`porting`](../../rust/porting/SKILL.md).

## 1. Principles

### 1.1 Rust consumers

A port produces a Rust library for Rust-native applications. Its public API is the safe
Rust one; the installed C headers and the C ABI they describe are not kept for C
applications outside the target. The crate bundles the C that remains, as
[`bindgen`](../../rust/bindgen/SKILL.md) describes, so that a consumer has the whole
library and reaches what is not ported yet through its raw bindings.

A ported module's C-facing surface is only what the target's own remaining C still
consumes, its translation units, tests and executables alike: its `extern "C"` exports,
under their bare C names, through which that C calls the Rust that replaced the module. The
remaining C depends on the Rust, never the Rust on a C copy of a ported module, so that
each function has one implementation and each global one copy. The surface shrinks as that
C is ported.

A type, public or internal, therefore keeps its C layout, and its `wrap`, only while
unported C of the target accesses that layout. The target's tests do not count, as
[Tests follow their modules](#12-tests-follow-their-modules) describes, and neither does a
definition in an installed header: the C consumers it would serve are outside the target.

### 1.2 Tests follow their modules

Each module carries the C tests tied to it, those whose subject it is, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Bundling section describes.
They assert the C contract, which a safe Rust implementation may change. Those that reach
the module's internals run while it is C and leave with it at its switch. Those that
use only its public API stay, and check its exports, which keep that contract for the C
that calls them, until their `port/unexport` carries them over, as the
[conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes. The tests its
port batches write mirror their regression cases, as
[`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s C tests carried over section describes. A
test's access to a module's internals is a use within that module, so it never keeps a type
wrapped.

A C test that only calls a module, to set up or tear down its fixtures, is not tied to it:
once the module has switched, the test reaches it through its exports, so that it checks
its own subject with the ported Rust under it, as part of the integration regression gate. A
test never keeps an export the remaining C no longer needs: the export's `port/unexport`
carries over the test cases that still reference it, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section describes.

A test whose subject is several modules is tied to each of them, and leaves at the first
point at which it would leave as a test of one of them alone. Each ported module's own
tests cover it from then on.

A test case whose body the configured build compiles empty, under a configuration the
target is built without, such as `GIT_WIN32`, tests nothing of the target: it is out of
scope, as a configured-out translation unit is, tied to no module and holding nothing back.

### 1.3 One language per module

A module is in one language at a time. The campaign maintains C and Rust side by side, but
on disjoint modules, never the same code in both.

While the waves of a module's `wrap` and `port` items run, its C is the reference its
ports are tested against, and the target is built and linked from C alone.
Once the last of them has landed, the module switches to Rust, once, as [Builds](#3-builds)
describes: the Rust module replaces the TU in the target's link, its C is removed from the
build and from the tree, and its tests switch with it. The removal is made on the working branch; the shipping branch keeps the C until
the user approves shipping the module. From then on the module is Rust's: what it still
keeps for the remaining C, its types' C layouts and storage and its exports, its later
stages remove after the switch, as [Later stages](#4-later-stages) describes.

The headers bundled with the module stay while remaining C includes them, declaring the
module's exports, its `static inline` functions included, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Static inline functions section describes, and go with the last C
file that includes them.

The module's equivalence tests, which need the C, are retired with it, and the behaviour
they established is kept by its unit tests. Before the module's equivalence tests are
retired, each that needs no C is carried over to the module's unit tests, where what it
compares with stays after the switch, such as the constants of a header that remaining C
still includes. The raw bindings of its
exported functions and globals then reach its exports, so that a consumer's raw calls keep
working, and an allowlist entry goes with the export it reaches. Those of its functions and
globals that have no export, which only its own C referenced, are removed with their
allowlist entries at the switch.

A ported module's items therefore reach the rest of its module natively from the start:
an edge within a module needs neither a `wrap` binding nor an export, only the edges that
leave it.

## 2. Batches

A port campaign's schedule mixes both kinds of batch, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s
Waves and batches section describes: a selected symbol is `port` from the start, a
selected type is `wrap` while another module's unported C depends on its layout and `port`
once none does, and a dependency outside the selected migration set stays `wrap`. A type
whose layout only its own module and tests use is `port` from the start. Each batch runs
the agent its objective names, in the same waves.

## 3. Builds

A module's waves do not change the compiled target. Its `port` batches add Rust that is
built and tested on its own, against the target's C build, which still compiles the
module's C and links no Rust: there is no build switch, and no batch flips one. The
module's `ffi_export` gateway is written with its items but compiled only under its export
feature, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports and Export features sections
describe, which stays off, so its bare-named exports never collide with the C the tests
link. Native Rust items carry mangled names and cannot collide with it.

The C stays until the switch: the target's other C still calls the module's symbols, which
only the exports could define, and the module's equivalence tests and its cut cycles still
run through it.

Once the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port` items has landed, it switches
in one step, with concurrent modules as part of its branch's integration into the working
branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Integration section
describes: its export feature is deleted, so that its gateway compiles from then on, its TU
and the C tests tied to it that reach its internals are removed from `c/`, and the
remaining C reaches the module through its exports. The C side of the
step is a commit on the fork's `main`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section
describes, and the campaign's commit records the submodule at it: integrations run one at a
time, so the two repositories move together.

The step's parts run in this order, both sides before the builds:

1. The Rust side, in one commit. The module's export feature is deleted, its equivalence
   tests are retired, those that need no C carried over first, the allowlist entries of its
   functions and globals that have no export are removed, and the bindings are regenerated
   against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not change.
   Deleting the feature removes or rewrites every mention of its name in the crate, in its
   sources, its tests, its manifest and its build script, a `cfg_attr` or a `cfg(any(…))`
   as much as the gateway's attribute: an unknown `cfg`, or a lint expectation left unmet,
   fails the lints with warnings denied.
2. The C side: the module's TU and its tied C tests leave the fork.
3. The builds, from the C that remains. Each variant is configured, the Rust library is
   built, then the C is built and linked: the C that remains links the module's exports,
   which the Rust library holds only once the export feature is deleted.
4. The gates, over those builds.

From then on, the C that remains is linked in two ways, and no process holds a module both
as C and as Rust, nor its Rust twice:

- a Rust consumer, the campaign's own tests included, links the safe crate and the C that
  remains, which the crate bundles, statically or as shared libraries, as the raw bindings'
  Build modes describe; and
- the target's remaining C consumers, its C tests and executables, link the C that remains
  and the safe crate's Rust static library, built in campaign mode so that it carries no C
  of its own, through the target's actual build system.

The C tests that remain run over that second link as the integration regression gate, as
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes.
For that link, the first switch changes the fork's C build so that the remaining C's
tests and executables link the safe crate's Rust library, static or shared, in the build
system's own idiom, and each later switch takes its module's C out of that build.

## 4. Later stages

A module switches once. Its later-stage waves, `port/layout`, `port/memory` and
`port/unexport`, run after its switch, each once the switches its release point
waits for have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section times them: as the remaining C stops using its types' layouts and storage and
calling its exports, they nativize the types and remove the exports. They belong to no run
of the module and integrate nothing: each forks from the working branch and is promoted
back to it, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section
describes. A stage changes no C, since the C that held it back has left the build, but for
what still names the export a `port/unexport` removes. That
change is a commit on the fork's `main`, which the stage's commit records, as a switch's
is, and the stage's C tests run over variants built from the C it leaves, as
[Builds](#3-builds) describes for a switch.

## 5. Scope

The unit of a port is a module: its scope is whole modules, the foundational ones
included, which stay `wrap`, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational modules section
describes. Porting a few named items without their module is not described.

Each module carries the C tests tied to it, those whose subject it is, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Bundling section describes.
They assert the C contract, which a safe Rust implementation may change. Those that reach
the module's internals run while it is C and leave with it at its switch. Those that
use only its public API stay, and check its exports, which keep that contract for the C
that calls them, until their `port/unexport` carries them over, as the
[conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports section describes. The tests its
port batches write mirror their regression cases, as
[`testing`](../../verification/testing/SKILL.md)'s C tests carried over section describes. A
test's access to a module's internals is a use within that module, so it never keeps a type
wrapped.

A C test that only calls a module, to set up or tear down its fixtures, is not tied to it:
once the module has switched, the test reaches it through its exports, so that it checks
its own subject with the ported Rust under it, as part of the integration regression gate. A
test never keeps an export the remaining C no longer needs: the export's `port/unexport`
carries over the test cases that still reference it, as
[`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages section describes.

A test whose subject is several modules is tied to each of them, and leaves at the first
point at which it would leave as a test of one of them alone. Each ported module's own
tests cover it from then on.

A test case whose body the configured build compiles empty, under a configuration the
target is built without, such as `GIT_WIN32`, tests nothing of the target: it is out of
scope, as a configured-out translation unit is, tied to no module and holding nothing back.

### 1.3 One language per module

A module is in one language at a time. The campaign maintains C and Rust side by side, but
on disjoint modules, never the same code in both.

While the waves of a module's `wrap` and `port` items run, its C is the reference its
ports are tested against, and the target is built and linked from C alone.
Once the last of them has landed, the module switches to Rust, once, as [Builds](#3-builds)
describes: the Rust module replaces the TU in the target's link, its C is removed from the
build and from the tree, and its tests switch with it. The removal is made on the working branch; the shipping branch keeps the C until
the user approves shipping the module. From then on the module is Rust's: what it still
keeps for the remaining C, its types' C layouts and storage and its exports, its later
stages remove after the switch, as [Later stages](#4-later-stages) describes.

The headers bundled with the module stay while remaining C includes them, declaring the
module's exports, its `static inline` functions included, as
[`porting-symbols`](../../rust/porting/symbols/SKILL.md)'s Static inline functions section describes, and go with the last C
file that includes them.

The module's equivalence tests, which need the C, are retired with it, and the behaviour
they established is kept by its unit tests. Before the module's equivalence tests are
retired, each that needs no C is carried over to the module's unit tests, where what it
compares with stays after the switch, such as the constants of a header that remaining C
still includes. The raw bindings of its
exported functions and globals then reach its exports, so that a consumer's raw calls keep
working, and an allowlist entry goes with the export it reaches. Those of its functions and
globals that have no export, which only its own C referenced, are removed with their
allowlist entries at the switch.

A ported module's items therefore reach the rest of its module natively from the start:
an edge within a module needs neither a `wrap` binding nor an export, only the edges that
leave it.

## 2. Batches

A port campaign's schedule mixes both kinds of batch, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s
Waves and batches section describes: a selected symbol is `port` from the start, a
selected type is `wrap` while another module's unported C depends on its layout and `port`
once none does, and a dependency outside the selected migration set stays `wrap`. A type
whose layout only its own module and tests use is `port` from the start. Each batch runs
the agent its objective names, in the same waves.

## 3. Builds

A module's waves do not change the compiled target. Its `port` batches add Rust that is
built and tested on its own, against the target's C build, which still compiles the
module's C and links no Rust: there is no build switch, and no batch flips one. The
module's `ffi_export` gateway is written with its items but compiled only under its export
feature, as the [conventions](../../rust/conventions/SKILL.md)' Exports and Export features sections
describe, which stays off, so its bare-named exports never collide with the C the tests
link. Native Rust items carry mangled names and cannot collide with it.

The C stays until the switch: the target's other C still calls the module's symbols, which
only the exports could define, and the module's equivalence tests and its cut cycles still
run through it.

Once the last wave of the module's `wrap` and `port` items has landed, it switches
in one step, with concurrent modules as part of its branch's integration into the working
branch, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Integration section
describes: its export feature is deleted, so that its gateway compiles from then on, its TU
and the C tests tied to it that reach its internals are removed from `c/`, and the
remaining C reaches the module through its exports. The C side of the
step is a commit on the fork's `main`, as
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Repositories section
describes, and the campaign's commit records the submodule at it: integrations run one at a
time, so the two repositories move together.

The step's parts run in this order, both sides before the builds:

1. The Rust side, in one commit. The module's export feature is deleted, its equivalence
   tests are retired, those that need no C carried over first, the allowlist entries of its
   functions and globals that have no export are removed, and the bindings are regenerated
   against the builds in use, whose headers the switch does not change.
   Deleting the feature removes or rewrites every mention of its name in the crate, in its
   sources, its tests, its manifest and its build script, a `cfg_attr` or a `cfg(any(…))`
   as much as the gateway's attribute: an unknown `cfg`, or a lint expectation left unmet,
   fails the lints with warnings denied.
2. The C side: the module's TU and its tied C tests leave the fork.
3. The builds, from the C that remains. Each variant is configured, the Rust library is
   built, then the C is built and linked: the C that remains links the module's exports,
   which the Rust library holds only once the export feature is deleted.
4. The gates, over those builds.

From then on, the C that remains is linked in two ways, and no process holds a module both
as C and as Rust, nor its Rust twice:

- a Rust consumer, the campaign's own tests included, links the safe crate and the C that
  remains, which the crate bundles, statically or as shared libraries, as the raw bindings'
  Build modes describe; and
- the target's remaining C consumers, its C tests and executables, link the C that remains
  and the safe crate's Rust static library, built in campaign mode so that it carries no C
  of its own, through the target's actual build system.

The C tests that remain run over that second link as the integration regression gate, as
[`testing-gates`](../../verification/testing/gates/SKILL.md)'s Regressions section describes.
For that link, the first switch changes the fork's C build so that the remaining C's
tests and executables link the safe crate's Rust library, static or shared, in the build
system's own idiom, and each later switch takes its module's C out of that build.

## 4. Later stages

A module switches once. Its later-stage waves, `port/layout`, `port/memory` and
`port/unexport`, run after its switch, each once the switches its release point
waits for have landed, as [`scheduling`](../../planning/scheduling/SKILL.md)'s Later stages
section times them: as the remaining C stops using its types' layouts and storage and
calling its exports, they nativize the types and remove the exports. They belong to no run
of the module and integrate nothing: each forks from the working branch and is promoted
back to it, as [`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Lifecycle section
describes. A stage changes no C, since the C that held it back has left the build, but for
what still names the export a `port/unexport` removes. That
change is a commit on the fork's `main`, which the stage's commit records, as a switch's
is, and the stage's C tests run over variants built from the C it leaves, as
[Builds](#3-builds) describes for a switch.

## 5. Scope

The unit of a port is a module: its scope is whole modules, the foundational ones
included, which stay `wrap`, as
[`decomposition`](../../planning/decomposition/SKILL.md)'s Foundational modules section
describes. Porting a few named items without their module is not described.

name: conventions
description: "Naming, tree layout, anchors and test placement of the Rust a campaign generates. Read before writing, homing or reviewing generated Rust or tests."
