# API stability per C item `ffimap api` measures a promise a C-to-Rust migration makes to its Rust consumers: once a C item has a safe Rust API, wrapping it, porting it and its later stages leave that API alone. It reads the crate's rustdoc JSON, finds the Rust items that stand in for each C item through their anchors, and records their consumer-facing surface twice: raw, as the signatures stand, and as the **contract** a consumer may rely on whatever form a handle or an owner takes. Two such records, one at the item's first landing and one after a later landing, say whether the contract was kept, extended or changed. This document is what the two documents hold and every rule behind them. The scan's counters are [`schema.md`](schema.md)'s and have nothing to do with it. ## 1. Input ```sh cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc -p CRATE --lib -- -Z unstable-options --output-format json (cd ffibox && cargo +nightly-2026-10-07 rustdoc --lib -- -Z unstable-options \ --output-format json --document-private-items) ffimap api extract target/doc/CRATE.json --dep ffibox/target/doc/ffibox.json > before.json ``` `--dep` gives the rustdoc JSON of a crate the measured one depends on, and is repeatable. The contracts of handles and owners that are aliases into ffibox (`CBox`, `CArc`, `CVal`, …) need ffibox's, since the reborrows and trait impls those forms inherit live there; it is made with `--document-private-items` because the bounds rustdoc synthesises for ffibox's auto-trait impls name its private fields' types. Without it those contracts are unresolved, as section 6 describes. The measure is pure Python over the JSON. It does not use the driver, so the crate need not build on the driver's nightly, only document on one whose JSON format it reads. Rustdoc's JSON is unstable: each nightly writes a `format_version`, and the shape moves with it. `ffimap api` reads **format 61**, which nightly-2026-10-07 (the driver's pin) and nightly-2026-10-08 emit, and refuses any other with an error naming the version it found. Support for a new format is added by checking the fields `src/ffimap/rustdoc.py` reads against it and adding it to `FORMAT_VERSIONS`. ## 2. C items and their stand-ins A C item is keyed by its anchor's `::`: `fn::git_mailmap_new`, `st::git_mailmap`, `fld::git_buf.ptr`. An anchor is a doc-comment line of its own, exactly ``Wraps `::` `` or ``Replaces `::` ``, where the path is names separated by dots and a `fld` path names a member. Every public item of the crate that carries one is a **stand-in** of that C item, and an item carrying several (the accessor of two members) is a stand-in of each. What the extract reports about the anchors themselves, under `anchors`: - `malformed`: a line that tries to be an anchor and is not one -- the verb and a `kind::` path inside a sentence, with a trailing period, without backticks, or with a path that is not names. It keys nothing. - `unknown_kinds`: anchors whose kind is not one of the convention's (`fn`, `st`, `un`, `enm`, `fnp`, `tdf`, `fld`, `glb`, `mac`), counted by kind. They are keyed as written. - `without_alias`: anchors on an item with no `#[doc(alias)]` naming the anchor's path. An item whose own name is the anchor's path is left out: rustdoc rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers a search for it. ## 3. Locators and paths Each stand-in is named by a **locator**, which is how one landing's record is matched with the next's: | item | locator | |---|---| | a free item | its canonical path | | an item of an inherent impl | `Ty::name` | | an item of a trait impl | `>::name` | | a trait's item, a variant, a field | its owner's locator `::name` | Lifetime names in a locator are erased to `'_`. A **canonical path** is the path a consumer names an item by. For an item of the crate it is the path rustdoc's `paths` table gives its definition when that path is public, else the shortest public path it is re-exported at, the first in order among equals. An item defined in a private module and re-exported from its parent is named by the parent's path, and a port that moves the definition into the parent changes nothing. An item of another crate is named by its definition's path in the `paths` table, `ffibox::refs::CBox` for instance, because this document does not record that crate's re-exports. Every type in a signature is rendered by its canonical path, never by what the source wrote, so an import or a reordering of the source gives the same bytes. A record's `paths` lists every public path the item is reached by, from the crate root through public modules and `pub use`, globs included. An associated item's are its owner's paths with its name appended. ## 4. Signatures Each stand-in's `sig` is normalised text by kind: - **functions and methods**: `decl` holds `const`, `async`, `unsafe`, the ABI, generics, the receiver (`self`, `&self`, `&'a mut self`, `self: Box`), the parameter types and return type, and where-clauses. A method also has the `impl` header it is declared in, generics and trait included, and a trait's method has `default`, whether it has a body. Parameter names are left out. - **structs, enums and unions**: `decl` holds the generics, the shape (`;`, `(n)`, `{}`) and `#[non_exhaustive]`. `fields` maps each public field to its type, and `variants` each variant to its shape and discriminant. `stripped` says whether rustdoc hid private fields or variants. `impls` maps the header of every trait impl rustdoc records for the type to its items (those it defines and the trait's provided ones it inherits) and its associated types and constants; the auto-trait impls rustdoc synthesises (`Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, and `Freeze` and `UnsafeUnpin` where the nightly records them), negative ones as `!Send`, are included, and blanket impls are not, since they follow from the type's other impls. `members` holds the items of its inherent impls that stand in for no C item, each with its impl header. - **traits**: `decl` with generics, supertraits and `unsafe`; `required` and `provided` items, each with its declaration; `dyn_compatible`. - **type aliases**: `decl` holds the whole target, `type = ffibox::refs::CBox<…>`. - **constants and statics**: type and value; **associated constants and types**: their declaration and, in an impl, its header; **variants** and **fields**: their shape or type; a `macro_rules!` macro only its kind, since its body is not an interface. A trait impl's methods are recorded by name only: their signatures are the trait's, recorded where the trait is. ## 5. Handles and owners The types a consumer reaches a C type through -- `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal` and a policy type such as `FooFree` -- are not always annotated. An unannotated public struct, enum, union or trait of the crate is **associated** with C items by rule 1, else by rule 2, and a type alias by rule 3; `via` says which rule tied it: 1. `assoc_type`: a trait impl of the type sets an associated type to an anchored type, or a trait impl of an anchored type sets one to it. `impl CRefSeam for MailmapRef { type Cell = Mailmap; }` and `impl CCell for Mailmap { type Ref<'a> = MailmapRef<'a>; }` both tie `MailmapRef` to `st::git_mailmap`. 2. `owner`: the type's impls, or the trait's declaration, hold stand-ins; it is associated with their C items. A policy type whose `CDrop::c_drop` wraps `fn::git_mailmap_free` goes with that item. 3. `alias`: a type alias whose target names an anchored type, by id anywhere in the target, goes with that type's C items: `MailmapBox = CBox` with `st::git_mailmap`. A target naming none goes with the items of the types it names that rules 1 and 2 associated. An associated item is recorded under each of its C items with the record a stand-in has, and a C item's surface is its stand-ins and its associated items together. ## 6. The contract view A handle or an owner changes form over a migration: `FooRef` is a pointer wrapper while `Foo` is wrapped and `&'a Foo` once it is ported, `FooBox` an ffibox `CBox` and then a `Box`. A consumer relies only on what every form offers, as `binding-types` states: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the native forms offer. The **contract** of a type is that, and it, not the raw record, decides a C item's status. Every C item has a `contract` view: one entry per stand-in or associated item. - **A type** (`Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal`, a policy type, an enum) has its contract under its locator: - `generics`: how many lifetimes, types and constants it takes; - `fields` (public ones), `shape` (only when a consumer can build it, no field hidden), `variants` and `non_exhaustive`; - `methods`: every method a consumer can call on it, by name, over every route: on the form itself, through its dereferences (`&self` methods through `Deref`, `&mut self` ones too through `DerefMut`) and on what its reborrows return. The route is not recorded, and the first found names a method; - `reborrows`: what `as_ref` and `as_mut` return. One returning the form's own type adds nothing and is left out; - `traits`: the traits it implements that a consumer can use, with their arguments; - `derefs`: targets reached through a dereference that the contract does not look inside (a slice, `str`, a primitive, a standard type), whose methods are the standard library's. - **A method of a handle or owner** is keyed `method::`, without its owner, since a port moves it from `FooRef` to `impl Foo`, and holds its normalised signatures. - **Any other function** has its normalised signature; anything else its raw record. Signatures in a contract are normalised so that each form reads the same: a type equal to the target of one of the crate's public aliases is written as the alias, so `&'a Foo` reads `FooRef<'_>` once `FooRef<'a> = &'a Foo`; lifetimes are erased; `Self` is the type the method is called on; a projection such as `::Ref<'_>` is resolved through `Foo`'s impl; parameter names are dropped; and a `self` receiver of a `Copy` type is `&self`. **What is no part of a contract:** | left out | why | |---|---| | functions without a `self` receiver | reached through a type path, which a change of form changes | | the seams `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr`, `from_void_ptr`, `from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `from_c`, `into_c`, `as_c_ptr`, `from_raw`, `as_object` | the conversion between a wrapper and its raw form, ffimap's seam list | | a method with a raw pointer or `NonNull` in its signature | raw access | | `unsafe` methods | they exist because a form wraps C; an anchored one is its own C item's | | anchored methods | each is its own C item's stand-in, compared there | | every method of a plumbing crate's type (`--plumbing`, ffibox by default) but `as_ref` and `as_mut` | what one form offers beyond the native ones, such as `try_clone` or `policy` | | the traits of a plumbing crate (`CCell`, `CDrop`, `CRefSeam`, …) | plumbing | | `Drop`, `StructuralPartialEq`, `Freeze`, `UnsafeUnpin` | no consumer can use them | | `Pointer` | it formats the address: raw access | | `Deref`, `DerefMut`, `AsRef`, `AsMut`, `Borrow`, `BorrowMut` | recorded as dereferences and reborrows, and through the methods they reach | | blanket impls | they follow from the others | **Where a form's surface comes from.** A type of the crate, or of a crate given with `--dep`, answers from its impls in that crate's JSON: an impl applies when its self type matches the form, and its bounds are checked against the impl lists rustdoc records (which list the blanket impls that apply), so `impl Send for CBox` holds for `CBox` exactly when `Foo` and `FooFree` are `Send`. A standard pointer form answers from a fixed model: `&T` and `&mut T` dereference to `T`, `Box` too, with `as_ref`/`as_mut`, `Arc` and `Rc` shared, `Pin

` as `P`, and each implements `Clone`, `Copy`, `Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, `Default`, `Debug`, `Display`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord` and `Hash` under the standard library's conditions on `T`; `NonNull` and `PhantomData` are modelled for the bounds they appear in. **Unresolved.** A contract that needs what is not there -- a type of a crate whose JSON was not given, a standard type the model does not cover, a bound that cannot be decided, such as one on the free parameter of a generic alias -- lists it under `unresolved`, and that entry is compared on its raw record instead (section 10). `contract_missing_deps` names the crates whose JSON would have resolved more. ## 7. The unattributed surface A public item of the crate that is neither a stand-in nor associated is **unattributed**. It is recorded by the Rust module of its canonical path, under `unattributed`, with the same records, and compared the same way, so a change to it is reported though no C item owns it. ## 8. Coverage `coverage` counts how far the anchors reach. `public` counts the crate's reachable items by role: free items by kind, `inherent_item` and `trait_impl_item` for the items of a type's impls (blanket and synthesised impls aside), `trait_item`, `variant` and `field`. `anchored` counts those that carry an anchor. `c_items` and `c_items_by_kind` count the keys, `stand_ins` the records, `associated` and `unattributed` the items those sections hold. ## 9. The extract ```json { "api": 2, "source": {"crate": "libgit2", "crate_version": "0.1.0", "format_version": 61, "deps": ["ffibox"], "plumbing": ["ffibox"]}, "items": { "st::git_mailmap": { "anchor": "Wraps", "stand_ins": {"libgit2::…::Mailmap": {"anchor": "Wraps", "kind": "struct", "paths": ["libgit2::…::Mailmap"], "sig": {…}}}, "associated": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type_alias", "via": ["alias"], "paths": […], "sig": {…}}}, "contract": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type", "generics": {…}, "methods": {…}, "reborrows": {…}, "traits": […]}, …} } }, "contract_missing_deps": [], "unattributed": {"libgit2::…::odb": {"libgit2::…::OdbDataStrVec": {…}}}, "anchors": {"malformed": [], "unknown_kinds": {}, "without_alias": []}, "coverage": {…} } ``` An item's `anchor` is its stand-ins' verb, or `mixed` when they differ. `api` is the extract's own version, bumped when a rule or the shape changes, and two extracts of different versions are not compared. Keys are sorted and the JSON is indented by one, so one document gives one byte sequence. ## 10. The diff `ffimap api diff BEFORE AFTER` takes two extracts, or two rustdoc JSON documents it extracts first (with the same `--dep` and `--plumbing`), and classifies every C item by its contract view: | status | when | |---|---| | `kept` | every entry is identical | | `extended` | only additions | | `changed` | anything lost or rewritten | | `removed` | the key is gone | | `new` | the key first appears | In the contract view an entry gained, a method, a reborrow, a trait, a dereference target, a signature beside a method's others, a field of a type with hidden fields or a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum is an addition; an entry, a method, a reborrow, a trait or a signature lost or rewritten, a generics count changed, and a field or variant gained where a consumer could build or match every one, is a change. A type whose raw record moved while its contract did not is a **retarget**: the item records `retarget` with the raw declarations before and after, and stays kept. `raw_status` says when the raw view would have classified the item otherwise. `--raw` classifies by the raw records instead, and an unresolved contract entry is compared on its raw record; the raw rules, where an addition and a change are: | addition (`extended`) | change (`changed`) | |---|---| | a stand-in or an associated item | a stand-in or an associated item lost, or its kind changed | | a public path | a public path lost | | a trait impl, auto traits included | a trait impl lost, auto traits included (`Send` becoming `!Send` is both) | | an item or associated type in a trait impl | one lost, or an associated type retargeted | | an inherent member no anchor claims | a member lost or rewritten | | a provided trait item, or a required one made provided | a required trait item, or any trait item lost or rewritten | | a field of a struct with private fields | a field of one without, or any field lost or retyped | | a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum | a variant of an exhaustive enum, or any variant lost or rewritten | | | a `decl` or `impl` header rewritten: a signature, an alias target, a constant's value | An item whose anchor verb moved records it as `anchor: {before, after}`, and `anchor_moves` counts the moves, so a wrap-to-port step reads `Wraps->Replaces` whatever the status. A key gone and a key come with the same path, one of each, are one C item whose anchor kind was relabelled: it is compared as one and records `rekeyed` with its old key. The JSON form, the default, holds the `view` that decided, `totals`, `anchor_moves`, `rekeyed`, `retargeted`, `unresolved`, every C item's `status` with its `changes`, `raw_status`, `retarget` and `unresolved`, and `unattributed` with its own totals by module, always on raw records. Each change names the entry's locator, the `part` that moved (`method`, `trait`, `reborrow`, `decl`, `impl`, `member`, `path`, …), whether it was `added`, `removed` or `changed`, its `severity` (`extended` or `changed`), the values before and after, and `view: raw` when an unresolved entry was compared raw. `--format text` prints the items that are neither kept nor new, with one line per change, then the totals. `--items` restricts the C items to a list of keys, a batch's worklist, and lists those found in neither document under `missing`. The unattributed surface is reported whatever it holds, since no worklist names it. ## 11. What the measure cannot see - **What no anchor reaches.** An unannotated type that no rule of section 5 ties to an anchored one is attributed to its module, not to a C item. - **The route to a method.** A contract flattens methods over dereferences and reborrows, so a method callable directly on one form and only through `as_ref()` on another reads the same. - **Lifetimes in contracts.** They are erased, so a getter returning a borrow of the handle and one returning a borrow of its target read the same. - **Standard types beyond the model.** A form that is an `Option`, a `Vec` or any standard type other than the pointer forms is unresolved, and so is a bound on a generic alias's free parameter. - **Behaviour.** A signature that stays while what the function does changes reads as kept. - **Renamed generics.** Generic parameter names are kept in declarations, so renaming `T` or a lifetime reads as changed, except in locators, where lifetimes are erased. - **Another crate's re-exports.** A dependency that moves a definition behind an unchanged re-export renders differently, since this document has only the definition's path. - **Semver nuance.** A change is anything lost or rewritten, whether or not a consumer could tell: a bound loosened or a where-clause reordered reads as changed. A contract's impl bounds are checked against impl lists only, one impl at a time, with no inference beyond what rustdoc recorded. - **Trait-impl method signatures.** They are the trait's; a change to an unanchored, unattributed trait is reported under its module only. - **Hidden items.** Rustdoc leaves `#[doc(hidden)]` items and private ones out of its JSON, so neither they nor anchors on them are seen. Without it those contracts are unresolved, as section 6 describes. The measure is pure Python over the JSON. It does not use the driver, so the crate need not build on the driver's nightly, only document on one whose JSON format it reads. Rustdoc's JSON is unstable: each nightly writes a `format_version`, and the shape moves with it. `ffimap api` reads **format 61**, which nightly-2026-10-07 (the driver's pin) and nightly-2026-10-08 emit, and refuses any other with an error naming the version it found. Support for a new format is added by checking the fields `src/ffimap/rustdoc.py` reads against it and adding it to `FORMAT_VERSIONS`. ## 2. C items and their stand-ins A C item is keyed by its anchor's `::`: `fn::git_mailmap_new`, `st::git_mailmap`, `fld::git_buf.ptr`. An anchor is a doc-comment line of its own, exactly ``Wraps `::` `` or ``Replaces `::` ``, where the path is names separated by dots and a `fld` path names a member. Every public item of the crate that carries one is a **stand-in** of that C item, and an item carrying several (the accessor of two members) is a stand-in of each. What the extract reports about the anchors themselves, under `anchors`: - `malformed`: a line that tries to be an anchor and is not one -- the verb and a `kind::` path inside a sentence, with a trailing period, without backticks, or with a path that is not names. It keys nothing. - `unknown_kinds`: anchors whose kind is not one of the convention's (`fn`, `st`, `un`, `enm`, `fnp`, `tdf`, `fld`, `glb`, `mac`), counted by kind. They are keyed as written. - `without_alias`: anchors on an item with no `#[doc(alias)]` naming the anchor's path. An item whose own name is the anchor's path is left out: rustdoc rejects an alias equal to its item's name, and the name already answers a search for it. ## 3. Locators and paths Each stand-in is named by a **locator**, which is how one landing's record is matched with the next's: | item | locator | |---|---| | a free item | its canonical path | | an item of an inherent impl | `Ty::name` | | an item of a trait impl | `>::name` | | a trait's item, a variant, a field | its owner's locator `::name` | Lifetime names in a locator are erased to `'_`. A **canonical path** is the path a consumer names an item by. For an item of the crate it is the path rustdoc's `paths` table gives its definition when that path is public, else the shortest public path it is re-exported at, the first in order among equals. An item defined in a private module and re-exported from its parent is named by the parent's path, and a port that moves the definition into the parent changes nothing. An item of another crate is named by its definition's path in the `paths` table, `ffibox::refs::CBox` for instance, because this document does not record that crate's re-exports. Every type in a signature is rendered by its canonical path, never by what the source wrote, so an import or a reordering of the source gives the same bytes. A record's `paths` lists every public path the item is reached by, from the crate root through public modules and `pub use`, globs included. An associated item's are its owner's paths with its name appended. ## 4. Signatures Each stand-in's `sig` is normalised text by kind: - **functions and methods**: `decl` holds `const`, `async`, `unsafe`, the ABI, generics, the receiver (`self`, `&self`, `&'a mut self`, `self: Box`), the parameter types and return type, and where-clauses. A method also has the `impl` header it is declared in, generics and trait included, and a trait's method has `default`, whether it has a body. Parameter names are left out. - **structs, enums and unions**: `decl` holds the generics, the shape (`;`, `(n)`, `{}`) and `#[non_exhaustive]`. `fields` maps each public field to its type, and `variants` each variant to its shape and discriminant. `stripped` says whether rustdoc hid private fields or variants. `impls` maps the header of every trait impl rustdoc records for the type to its items (those it defines and the trait's provided ones it inherits) and its associated types and constants; the auto-trait impls rustdoc synthesises (`Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, and `Freeze` and `UnsafeUnpin` where the nightly records them), negative ones as `!Send`, are included, and blanket impls are not, since they follow from the type's other impls. `members` holds the items of its inherent impls that stand in for no C item, each with its impl header. - **traits**: `decl` with generics, supertraits and `unsafe`; `required` and `provided` items, each with its declaration; `dyn_compatible`. - **type aliases**: `decl` holds the whole target, `type = ffibox::refs::CBox<…>`. - **constants and statics**: type and value; **associated constants and types**: their declaration and, in an impl, its header; **variants** and **fields**: their shape or type; a `macro_rules!` macro only its kind, since its body is not an interface. A trait impl's methods are recorded by name only: their signatures are the trait's, recorded where the trait is. ## 5. Handles and owners The types a consumer reaches a C type through -- `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal` and a policy type such as `FooFree` -- are not always annotated. An unannotated public struct, enum, union or trait of the crate is **associated** with C items by rule 1, else by rule 2, and a type alias by rule 3; `via` says which rule tied it: 1. `assoc_type`: a trait impl of the type sets an associated type to an anchored type, or a trait impl of an anchored type sets one to it. `impl CRefSeam for MailmapRef { type Cell = Mailmap; }` and `impl CCell for Mailmap { type Ref<'a> = MailmapRef<'a>; }` both tie `MailmapRef` to `st::git_mailmap`. 2. `owner`: the type's impls, or the trait's declaration, hold stand-ins; it is associated with their C items. A policy type whose `CDrop::c_drop` wraps `fn::git_mailmap_free` goes with that item. 3. `alias`: a type alias whose target names an anchored type, by id anywhere in the target, goes with that type's C items: `MailmapBox = CBox` with `st::git_mailmap`. A target naming none goes with the items of the types it names that rules 1 and 2 associated. An associated item is recorded under each of its C items with the record a stand-in has, and a C item's surface is its stand-ins and its associated items together. ## 6. The contract view A handle or an owner changes form over a migration: `FooRef` is a pointer wrapper while `Foo` is wrapped and `&'a Foo` once it is ported, `FooBox` an ffibox `CBox` and then a `Box`. A consumer relies only on what every form offers, as `binding-types` states: their methods, their reborrows (`as_ref`, `as_mut`) and the dereferences the native forms offer. The **contract** of a type is that, and it, not the raw record, decides a C item's status. Every C item has a `contract` view: one entry per stand-in or associated item. - **A type** (`Foo`, `FooRef`, `FooMut`, `FooBox`, `FooArc`, `FooVal`, a policy type, an enum) has its contract under its locator: - `generics`: how many lifetimes, types and constants it takes; - `fields` (public ones), `shape` (only when a consumer can build it, no field hidden), `variants` and `non_exhaustive`; - `methods`: every method a consumer can call on it, by name, over every route: on the form itself, through its dereferences (`&self` methods through `Deref`, `&mut self` ones too through `DerefMut`) and on what its reborrows return. The route is not recorded, and the first found names a method; - `reborrows`: what `as_ref` and `as_mut` return. One returning the form's own type adds nothing and is left out; - `traits`: the traits it implements that a consumer can use, with their arguments; - `derefs`: targets reached through a dereference that the contract does not look inside (a slice, `str`, a primitive, a standard type), whose methods are the standard library's. - **A method of a handle or owner** is keyed `method::`, without its owner, since a port moves it from `FooRef` to `impl Foo`, and holds its normalised signatures. - **Any other function** has its normalised signature; anything else its raw record. Signatures in a contract are normalised so that each form reads the same: a type equal to the target of one of the crate's public aliases is written as the alias, so `&'a Foo` reads `FooRef<'_>` once `FooRef<'a> = &'a Foo`; lifetimes are erased; `Self` is the type the method is called on; a projection such as `::Ref<'_>` is resolved through `Foo`'s impl; parameter names are dropped; and a `self` receiver of a `Copy` type is `&self`. **What is no part of a contract:** | left out | why | |---|---| | functions without a `self` receiver | reached through a type path, which a change of form changes | | the seams `as_ptr`, `as_mut_ptr`, `as_void_ptr`, `from_ptr`, `from_void_ptr`, `from_raw_parts`, `into_raw_parts`, `from_c`, `into_c`, `as_c_ptr`, `from_raw`, `as_object` | the conversion between a wrapper and its raw form, ffimap's seam list | | a method with a raw pointer or `NonNull` in its signature | raw access | | `unsafe` methods | they exist because a form wraps C; an anchored one is its own C item's | | anchored methods | each is its own C item's stand-in, compared there | | every method of a plumbing crate's type (`--plumbing`, ffibox by default) but `as_ref` and `as_mut` | what one form offers beyond the native ones, such as `try_clone` or `policy` | | the traits of a plumbing crate (`CCell`, `CDrop`, `CRefSeam`, …) | plumbing | | `Drop`, `StructuralPartialEq`, `Freeze`, `UnsafeUnpin` | no consumer can use them | | `Pointer` | it formats the address: raw access | | `Deref`, `DerefMut`, `AsRef`, `AsMut`, `Borrow`, `BorrowMut` | recorded as dereferences and reborrows, and through the methods they reach | | blanket impls | they follow from the others | **Where a form's surface comes from.** A type of the crate, or of a crate given with `--dep`, answers from its impls in that crate's JSON: an impl applies when its self type matches the form, and its bounds are checked against the impl lists rustdoc records (which list the blanket impls that apply), so `impl Send for CBox` holds for `CBox` exactly when `Foo` and `FooFree` are `Send`. A standard pointer form answers from a fixed model: `&T` and `&mut T` dereference to `T`, `Box` too, with `as_ref`/`as_mut`, `Arc` and `Rc` shared, `Pin

` as `P`, and each implements `Clone`, `Copy`, `Send`, `Sync`, `Unpin`, `UnwindSafe`, `RefUnwindSafe`, `Default`, `Debug`, `Display`, `PartialEq`, `Eq`, `PartialOrd`, `Ord` and `Hash` under the standard library's conditions on `T`; `NonNull` and `PhantomData` are modelled for the bounds they appear in. **Unresolved.** A contract that needs what is not there -- a type of a crate whose JSON was not given, a standard type the model does not cover, a bound that cannot be decided, such as one on the free parameter of a generic alias -- lists it under `unresolved`, and that entry is compared on its raw record instead (section 10). `contract_missing_deps` names the crates whose JSON would have resolved more. ## 7. The unattributed surface A public item of the crate that is neither a stand-in nor associated is **unattributed**. It is recorded by the Rust module of its canonical path, under `unattributed`, with the same records, and compared the same way, so a change to it is reported though no C item owns it. ## 8. Coverage `coverage` counts how far the anchors reach. `public` counts the crate's reachable items by role: free items by kind, `inherent_item` and `trait_impl_item` for the items of a type's impls (blanket and synthesised impls aside), `trait_item`, `variant` and `field`. `anchored` counts those that carry an anchor. `c_items` and `c_items_by_kind` count the keys, `stand_ins` the records, `associated` and `unattributed` the items those sections hold. ## 9. The extract ```json { "api": 2, "source": {"crate": "libgit2", "crate_version": "0.1.0", "format_version": 61, "deps": ["ffibox"], "plumbing": ["ffibox"]}, "items": { "st::git_mailmap": { "anchor": "Wraps", "stand_ins": {"libgit2::…::Mailmap": {"anchor": "Wraps", "kind": "struct", "paths": ["libgit2::…::Mailmap"], "sig": {…}}}, "associated": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type_alias", "via": ["alias"], "paths": […], "sig": {…}}}, "contract": {"libgit2::…::MailmapBox": {"kind": "type", "generics": {…}, "methods": {…}, "reborrows": {…}, "traits": […]}, …} } }, "contract_missing_deps": [], "unattributed": {"libgit2::…::odb": {"libgit2::…::OdbDataStrVec": {…}}}, "anchors": {"malformed": [], "unknown_kinds": {}, "without_alias": []}, "coverage": {…} } ``` An item's `anchor` is its stand-ins' verb, or `mixed` when they differ. `api` is the extract's own version, bumped when a rule or the shape changes, and two extracts of different versions are not compared. Keys are sorted and the JSON is indented by one, so one document gives one byte sequence. ## 10. The diff `ffimap api diff BEFORE AFTER` takes two extracts, or two rustdoc JSON documents it extracts first (with the same `--dep` and `--plumbing`), and classifies every C item by its contract view: | status | when | |---|---| | `kept` | every entry is identical | | `extended` | only additions | | `changed` | anything lost or rewritten | | `removed` | the key is gone | | `new` | the key first appears | In the contract view an entry gained, a method, a reborrow, a trait, a dereference target, a signature beside a method's others, a field of a type with hidden fields or a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum is an addition; an entry, a method, a reborrow, a trait or a signature lost or rewritten, a generics count changed, and a field or variant gained where a consumer could build or match every one, is a change. A type whose raw record moved while its contract did not is a **retarget**: the item records `retarget` with the raw declarations before and after, and stays kept. `raw_status` says when the raw view would have classified the item otherwise. `--raw` classifies by the raw records instead, and an unresolved contract entry is compared on its raw record; the raw rules, where an addition and a change are: | addition (`extended`) | change (`changed`) | |---|---| | a stand-in or an associated item | a stand-in or an associated item lost, or its kind changed | | a public path | a public path lost | | a trait impl, auto traits included | a trait impl lost, auto traits included (`Send` becoming `!Send` is both) | | an item or associated type in a trait impl | one lost, or an associated type retargeted | | an inherent member no anchor claims | a member lost or rewritten | | a provided trait item, or a required one made provided | a required trait item, or any trait item lost or rewritten | | a field of a struct with private fields | a field of one without, or any field lost or retyped | | a variant of a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum | a variant of an exhaustive enum, or any variant lost or rewritten | | | a `decl` or `impl` header rewritten: a signature, an alias target, a constant's value | An item whose anchor verb moved records it as `anchor: {before, after}`, and `anchor_moves` counts the moves, so a wrap-to-port step reads `Wraps->Replaces` whatever the status. A key gone and a key come with the same path, one of each, are one C item whose anchor kind was relabelled: it is compared as one and records `rekeyed` with its old key. The JSON form, the default, holds the `view` that decided, `totals`, `anchor_moves`, `rekeyed`, `retargeted`, `unresolved`, every C item's `status` with its `changes`, `raw_status`, `retarget` and `unresolved`, and `unattributed` with its own totals by module, always on raw records. Each change names the entry's locator, the `part` that moved (`method`, `trait`, `reborrow`, `decl`, `impl`, `member`, `path`, …), whether it was `added`, `removed` or `changed`, its `severity` (`extended` or `changed`), the values before and after, and `view: raw` when an unresolved entry was compared raw. `--format text` prints the items that are neither kept nor new, with one line per change, then the totals. `--items` restricts the C items to a list of keys, a batch's worklist, and lists those found in neither document under `missing`. The unattributed surface is reported whatever it holds, since no worklist names it. ## 11. What the measure cannot see - **What no anchor reaches.** An unannotated type that no rule of section 5 ties to an anchored one is attributed to its module, not to a C item. - **The route to a method.** A contract flattens methods over dereferences and reborrows, so a method callable directly on one form and only through `as_ref()` on another reads the same. - **Lifetimes in contracts.** They are erased, so a getter returning a borrow of the handle and one returning a borrow of its target read the same. - **Standard types beyond the model.** A form that is an `Option`, a `Vec` or any standard type other than the pointer forms is unresolved, and so is a bound on a generic alias's free parameter. - **Behaviour.** A signature that stays while what the function does changes reads as kept. - **Renamed generics.** Generic parameter names are kept in declarations, so renaming `T` or a lifetime reads as changed, except in locators, where lifetimes are erased. - **Another crate's re-exports.** A dependency that moves a definition behind an unchanged re-export renders differently, since this document has only the definition's path. - **Semver nuance.** A change is anything lost or rewritten, whether or not a consumer could tell: a bound loosened or a where-clause reordered reads as changed. A contract's impl bounds are checked against impl lists only, one impl at a time, with no inference beyond what rustdoc recorded. - **Trait-impl method signatures.** They are the trait's; a change to an unanchored, unattributed trait is reported under its module only. - **Hidden items.** Rustdoc leaves `#[doc(hidden)]` items and private ones out of its JSON, so neither they nor anchors on them are seen. # The packaging gate's command is worked out by hand

Status: `superseded` by `package-gate-procedure`, on 2026-11-14: the same signal, which that
proposal states more widely. The command that passed here is copied into it.

## Signal

A procedure I had to work out by hand, over three failed runs, that the gate names but does
not give.

## Evidence

`wave-186/batch-0/run-1` changed the raw bindings (`sys/git2/allowlist.txt`). Per
`testing-gates`' Regressions section, that means it packages the safe crate "built alone in
bundled mode … each crate the package depends on … patched to its local source". Run from
the worktree with `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT=` and `--allow-dirty`:

1. `cargo package` failed: `no matching package named glibc-bindings found` (crates.io). The
   manifest's `[patch."https://github.com/crustify-rs/…"]` does not apply to the packaged
   manifest, whose dependencies are registry ones. The fix was
   `--config 'patch.crates-io.glibc-bindings.path="/target/glibc-crustify"'
   --config 'patch.crates-io.ffibox.path="/crustify-rs/ffibox"'`.
2. The bundled CMake configure then failed: `PCRE2 support was requested but not found`, and
   after that `system zlib was requested but not found`. The side campaigns' installs
   (`<repo>/../{openssl,pcre2,zlib}-bindings/crustify/builds/plain/install`) have to be on
   `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`, and colon-separated, since that is the environment variable's form.
   The `plain` variant's `configure` in `build.json` passes them semicolon-separated, as a
   `-D` value, and copying that form failed.

With both changes, the crate packaged 698 files and verified.

## Destination

A campaign artifact the assistant owns: a script beside `crustify/scripts/cargo-variant.sh`
(such as `crustify/scripts/package.sh`) that runs the gate with the patches derived from the
manifest's `[patch]` sections and the side installs from `build.json`'s `plain` prefix path.
Its use would then go in `testing-gates`' Regressions section, or in a lesson until the
wrappers are published.

## Change

Not made: neither file is the translator's. The command that passed:

```bash
S=$(realpath -m crustify/builds/plain/../../../..)
I() { echo "$S/$1-bindings/crustify/builds/plain/install"; }
CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT= OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR=$(I openssl) \
CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$(I openssl):$(I pcre2):$(I zlib)" \
PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$(I pcre2)/lib/pkgconfig:$(I zlib)/lib/pkgconfig" \
cargo package --allow-dirty \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.glibc-bindings.path="/target/glibc-crustify"' \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.ffibox.path="/crustify-rs/ffibox"'
```

## Validation

The command above packaged and verified the tree of `wave-186/batch-0`. The two earlier
forms failed as quoted.

## Review

None yet.

PROPOSAL.md
# The packaging gate's procedure, for a crate whose dependencies are unpublished
Status: `open`.
## Signal
A procedure worked out by hand that a skill should state: `testing-gates`' Regressions
section says that a batch that changes the raw bindings packages the safe crate, "built
alone in bundled mode from the C it packages, with no build variant selected", and that
"each crate the package depends on is patched to its local source", but not how. The
direct form fails, and the steps that pass were found by trial.
## Evidence
`wave-229/batch-0/run-1` (`src/util/utf8.c`, which allowlists three functions), on base
`2216b0cd0`, the first packaging gate since the tree's change of 2026-11-13:
1. `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT= cargo package --offline --allow-dirty` stops before verifying:
   `no matching package named glibc-bindings found` (crates.io index). The packaged
   manifest drops the Git source of `glibc-bindings` and the path of `ffibox`, keeping
   their versions, and the workspace's `[patch]` tables, keyed by those sources, do not
   apply to it.
2. `cargo package --offline --allow-dirty --no-verify --exclude-lockfile` packages (697
   files). Extracted under `crustify/tmp/`, the package's manifest needs an empty
   `[workspace]`, since the worktree's own encloses it, and
   `[patch.crates-io] glibc-bindings = { path = "/target/glibc-crustify" }` and
   `ffibox = { path = "/crustify-rs/ffibox" }`.
3. `CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT= cargo build --offline` there then fails in CMake: PCRE2, then
   zlib, not found. The host has neither: the bundled build finds them only through the
   side campaigns' `plain` installs, `OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR` and `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH`, the
   latter `:`-separated in the environment where `build.json`'s `-D` form takes `;`.
   With `OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR=<openssl install>` and
   `CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH=<openssl install>:<pcre2 install>:<zlib install>`, the package
   builds alone: cmake builds `libgit2.a` and `libcrustify_git2.a` into `OUT_DIR`.
`modules/git2/src/cli/opt.c/integration/run-1` (the switch of `src/cli/opt.c`, on
`f68ea8660`), the next packaging gate, followed steps 2 and 3 and failed to compile the
package's `lib`: two copies of ffibox, `0.1.1` by path for the crate and `0.1.0` by Git
(`40621a2`) for `glibc-bindings`, whose manifest takes ffibox by Git. The workspace patches
that Git source too (`[patch."https://github.com/crustify-rs/ffibox"]`), and step 2's
`[patch.crates-io]` does not stand for it. `opt.rs`'s gateway, which compiles from this switch
on, is the first code of the crate to pass a `glibc_bindings` `FileRef` through the crate's
own ffibox traits (`FileRef::from_ptr`, E0599 four times), so `utf8.c`'s gate could not have
met it. With the workspace's Git patch copied into the package's manifest as well, and the
lockfile the first attempt wrote removed, so that the patch applies, the graph holds one
ffibox and the package builds alone (696 files). Its `lib` tests: 829 pass and 58 fail, the
58 needing `c/tests/resources`, as at `utf8.c`'s gate. So the script copies every `[patch]`
table of the workspace, the Git sources' as well as crates.io's, and resolves with no
lockfile.
## Destination
The spec: `testing-gates`' Regressions section, with a script beside it, as `authoring`
places a procedure that must run exactly so, documented by its `--help`: it packages
without verifying, patches each unpublished dependency to the source the workspace's
`[patch]` names for it, gives the extracted package a workspace of its own, puts the
out-of-tree libraries' installs of the `plain` variant on the build system's search paths,
and builds it with no variant, in a scratch dir it removes.
## Change
Not made: the gate is not a translator's to change. The section would name the script,
and say that the patches and search paths stand in for what a dependent's host supplies.
From `packaging-gate-procedure`, which this proposal supersedes: the command that packaged and
verified the tree of `wave-186/batch-0`, after two forms that failed:
```bash
S=$(realpath -m crustify/builds/plain/../../../..)
I() { echo "$S/$1-bindings/crustify/builds/plain/install"; }
CRUSTIFY_BUILD_VARIANT= OPENSSL_ROOT_DIR=$(I openssl) \
CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH="$(I openssl):$(I pcre2):$(I zlib)" \
PKG_CONFIG_PATH="$(I pcre2)/lib/pkgconfig:$(I zlib)/lib/pkgconfig" \
cargo package --allow-dirty \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.glibc-bindings.path="/target/glibc-crustify"' \
  --config 'patch.crates-io.ffibox.path="/crustify-rs/ffibox"'
```
## Validation
The run above, step by step: step 1 fails as quoted, steps 2 and 3 pass. A script is
validated by passing on that tree and failing, naming the library, without the search
paths.

---
name: evolution
description: "How Crustify repairs and improves itself from what its campaigns expose: goals, signals, proposals, lessons, evolution branches, validation, review, autonomy, adoption, and where the record of what landed is kept. Read before filing a defect in Crustify or a tool, proposing or making a change to either, or recording a campaign's lesson; `evolution-record` holds the record and how evolution itself evolves."
---

# Evolution

How a campaign changes the harness that runs it, Crustify's skills, agents, templates and
providers, its tools and the tools it lacks, and how its agents propose changes to the
campaign's artifacts that other roles own. A campaign exposes what the harness gets
wrong, what it constrains needlessly and what it repeats by hand; evolution turns that
evidence into changes, under the autonomy the settings' `evolution` answer grants, and
this guidance itself among them. Where a change goes within Crustify is
[`authoring`](../authoring/SKILL.md)'s.

## 1. Goals

Every change is judged against Crustify's goals, [`GOALS.md`](../../../GOALS.md), read in
full before the first proposal: a change serves one of them, or it is not made. The goals
are evolved too, when the evidence questions them, as `GOALS.md` describes.

A change to a tool is judged against that tool's own goals and non-goals too, the document

| review findings that recur across batches, in one objective or category | a rule the how-to skills lack |
| failed or rerun batches, and plan corrections | a defect in planning, scheduling or packing |
| the user's corrections | a rule, or a lesson of the campaign |
| cost or time outliers, in the dashboard | waste in batch sizing, gates or tooling |
| one representation hand-written in several places, or a TODO met again and again | a primitive or tool feature that is missing |
| one procedure repeated by hand: the same script written again, the same queries run in sequence | a tool, or a subcommand of one |
| a signal evolution missed, or a proposal that proved wrong | a defect in this guidance |
| a goal no decision cites, two that keep conflicting the same way, or a well-founded change no goal serves | a change to the goals |

finding, a workaround or a measured waste. Fewer, well-founded proposals serve better than
many small ones: a change made for style alone, or for completeness, or to have proposed
something, is not made.

## 3. Destinations

Each signal goes to one destination:

- **the campaign alone**: what a setting or a task message settles, which changes nothing
  of Crustify;
- **a lesson**: a rule that holds for this target alone, recorded in the campaign's
  [`LESSONS.md`](#5-lessons);
- **the spec**: a skill, an agent, a template or a provider, where `authoring` places it;
- **a tool**: its code, its documentation or its tests, or a new tool; or
- **a campaign artifact**: the plan, the dependencies, the schedule or the dashboard, where
  the evidence shows one wrong or improvable and another role owns it. Its owner applies
  the proposal or declines it, a plan's at the next planner run.

blocked, or a launch mode that withholds what the role needs, is a defect of that host's
provider, not of the rule: the provider prevents it with whatever its host offers, its
agents' definitions, the settings and permissions it installs, its hooks, the mode it
launches runs in, or the host's memory, and the spec is not bent around one host. Until
the provider's change lands, a run that meets the refusal neither works around it nor drops
what it could not do: it hands that to the assistant, in its final message, and the
assistant carries it out.

the target's own names is a lesson, and one the spec takes is stated without them, as it
would hold for any C codebase.

## 4. Proposals

A proposal is filed in the campaign's repository under `crustify/evolution/<slug>/`, as its
`PROPOSAL.md`. It states:

- the signal and its evidence, with the runs, findings and commits it cites;
- the goal it serves, by name, and the fitness measure of that goal it expects to move;
- its destination;
- the change, or the patch;
- how it was validated;
- the row the record takes when the change lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes;
- its review's verdict; and
- its status: `open`; `deferred`, with what it waits for; `landed`, with the commit it
  landed as; `declined`, with why; or `superseded`, with the proposal that replaces it.

proposal: its slug, its signal in a line, its status, the runs that met the signal, and the
row of the record it matches, if any. The index has one writer per campaign, so that two
runs never write a row at once. It is written as each batch's proposals land, and holds
every proposal of the campaign before a wave launches.

index, in its worktree, and the record, in Crustify's checkout. Campaigns that share a
component's working branch, as a side campaign does with its parent, read each other's index
too:

- where the index holds its signal in a proposal that is `open` or `deferred`, the run files
  nothing new. When that proposal is in the run's own repository, the run adds its evidence
  to it, as an occurrence; otherwise, the run reports the occurrence in its final message,
  and the index's writer records it;
- otherwise, where its signal meets the recurrence signal of a row of the record, the change
  that landed did not hold: the run files a new proposal that cites the row, as
  [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s Record section describes; and
- otherwise, the run files the proposal.

while reviewing is a proposal, not a finding on the reviewed code, and is filed with its
reproducer.

before its first step. Each lesson is one entry, under a heading that is its id: a short
slug no other lesson of the file has. An entry holds a status, one rule, the evidence the
rule rests on, and, on a line of its own, its scope: the modules, items or stages it holds
for.

  commit that added or changed it reads it, against its evidence, its scope and the
  generality test of [Destinations](#3-destinations). A lesson no worklist holds, such as
  one a wave's last review batch adds, is read by the next review batch the campaign
  launches.
- The review batch that reads a lesson marks it `held` in its landing. A lesson it judges
  wrong, or one that belongs in the spec, is a finding of that batch: under `fix`, the
  batch corrects the entry, retires it, or files the proposal it should have been.
- A lesson the code no longer supports is `retired`. It stays in the file, marked, with
  why.
- An edit changes one entry. The file is never rewritten whole, since a rewrite drops what
  its writer did not think to keep.

since the last pass: duplicates are merged, stale lessons are retired, scopes are checked,
and a lesson that can be stated without the target's names is proposed for the spec, as is
one a second campaign records again, by a proposal citing both. A lesson the pass changes
is `provisional` again.

that component's repository, `<campaign-id>/devel`, the campaign id being the name of the
campaign's repository. It is forked from the component's `devel` when the campaign first
needs it, and the campaign's runs read and run the component from its checkout, so that a
campaign runs on what it has changed and no other campaign does.

working branch, in a worktree beside the repository that lives only while the change is
made. A branch holds one concern. Once the change lands on the working branch, by a

  that describes its use, as `authoring` places one; a tool of its own repository is

landed on the working branch as soon as it is reviewed, rather than batched.

A tool's change is validated by its tests, the regression test it adds among them.

the batch or the stage, under the change: a lightweight run, without the tests or gates
the failure does not need to show. The proposal records what the run produced before and
after, and a change whose rerun still fails does not land. A spec change no failure
prompted, such as a rule loosened or a waste removed, is validated the same way where its
effect is in doubt, on the item its evidence came from.

watched in the campaigns after it lands, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes.

change is reviewed before the next wave of its campaign launches, so that later runs work on

- the change serves a goal, and a tool's stays within the tool's own goals;

- its validation was run, and shows what the proposal says;
- the row its proposal drafts for the record, as [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) describes, names a recurrence

exception, where each file the commit changes is the same in the rebased commit and its

|---|---|

loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;

  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`

protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

role's; the task message of the run that asks for it adds to them, and never relaxes them.
A review reads as deeply as the change reaches: a change to documentation alone is read; a
tool's code, a check, a soundness fix and every rule of the spec are reviewed with their
validation run again.

The verdict is recorded in the proposal's Review section, approved or rejected, with its
reasons; a rejection leaves the proposal open for another change or for the user.

What only records what was decided changes no rule and is not reviewed: a row of the index,
a status of the record, or a proposal's status, verdict and review. A row of the record is
reviewed in its proposal, with its change.

A change that weakens a check, a gate, a test, a lint, a review objective, a tool's
detection or a rule of this skill, is marked so in the verdict and in its entry of the
record, since a run that can loosen what judges it passes by loosening it: the user reads
each such change on its own before `devel` takes it, as [Autonomy](#9-autonomy) describes.

## 9. Autonomy

The settings' `evolution` answer sets how far a campaign evolves the harness:

| answer | what lands on the campaign's working branches |
|---|---|
| `off` | nothing: no proposal, no lesson |
| `propose` | nothing but the index's rows and the record's statuses: proposals and lessons are filed, and no rule changes |
| `repair` | each fix of a defect |
| `evolve` | also each improvement and discovery |

A change lands on its component's working branch as soon as its review approves it, without
the user's approval: the working branch is the campaign's own, and nothing else runs on it.

The protected paths are the exception. They hold what judges the work, and a run that can
loosen what judges it passes by loosening it. In Crustify's repository they are:

- `GOALS.md`;
- `skills/crustify/evolution/**` and `skills/verification/**`, the scripts beside those
  skills included;
- `skills/artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md`;
- the Lints and Unsafe code sections of `skills/rust/toolchain/SKILL.md`;
- the Testing, Reviewing and Audit sections of `skills/tools/*/SKILL.md`, and every section
  of one that describes a scan a landing passes, such as `ffimap`'s Binding › Safe boundary;
- `agents/common.md`, `agents/reviewer.md` and the Evolution section of
  `agents/assistant/assistant.md`;
- the `evolution` question of `templates/*/CRUSTIFY.template.md`;
- `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, which decides the skills and hooks a run loads; and
- `providers/generic/compose.py` and, under `providers/claude/`, `compose.py`, `spawn.py`,
  `system-prompt.md`, `hooks.json` and `agents/*.md`. A generated agent that changes only as
  its sources outside this list changed is not a change to a protected path.

A change whose diff touches a protected path lands on the working branch only with the
user's approval, whatever its review says, and so does the removal of a `weakens a check`
mark from the record. One case lands without that approval: the repair of a defect in
protected code, a script or a provider's program, that blocks the campaign, once its review
approves it and finds three things. The repair weakens no check. Every existing test of the
code it touches is unchanged. The repair adds a regression test of its own. Such a repair is
put to the user at the next module's end. A change to a protected text always waits for the
user. A
change to `GOALS.md` is proposed and never made, unless the user asks for it, since
`GOALS.md` is what every other change is judged against.

A component's `devel` is the user's gate. It takes a campaign's working branch only with
the user's approval, asked for at each module's end and at the campaign's end, with the
record's entries since the last advance, those the review marked as weakening a check
first. Where `devel` has moved meanwhile, the working branch takes it by merge before it
is offered. What the user declines is reverted on the working branch or stays there, as
they say, and is recorded so; where it weakened a check, what landed under it is reviewed
again, by review batches with `revisit`, as [Adoption](#10-adoption) schedules them for a
soundness fix. Merging a component's `devel` into its `main`, and merging a
new tool upstream, need the user's approval too.

A run that a defect blocks does not work around it. Where the answer lets fixes land, it
makes the fix on its evolution branch; under `propose` it files the proposal, with its
reproducer, and the user is asked at once whether the fix is to be made; and it ends,
reporting which. The fix is reviewed and lands, and the run is run again, as a failed
batch is.

## 10. Adoption

Every run's `task.json` records the revisions of Crustify and the tools it launched
under, as [`task-schema`](../../artifacts/task-schema/SKILL.md)'s Run fields section
describes. A change that lands on a working branch takes effect as it lands: the runs launched
after it record its revision, and a run under way when it lands, which its recorded
revisions and its landing's date tell, may have followed either. What landed before it
under the old rules stays, unless the change fixes a soundness
defect: then the landings it affects are reviewed again, by a review batch with
`revisit`.

At each module's end, the campaign's evolution is consolidated: open proposals are landed
as the autonomy allows, the working branches are offered to the user for `devel`, and the
revisit batches a soundness fix or a declined weakening calls for are scheduled. The
lessons are reconciled when [Lessons](#5-lessons) times it, and the record's rows are read
when [`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md) times it.

## 11. The record

The record of what landed, `EVOLUTION.md`, and how evolution itself evolves from it are
[`evolution-record`](record/SKILL.md)'s.

---
name: authoring
description: "How Crustify itself is organized: skills, roles, tool skills and the plugin, where each kind of text goes, and the language every text is written in. Read before changing Crustify, filing a proposal or a lesson, or writing a task message for an agent."
---

# Authoring

How Crustify is organized: its skills, its agents and the providers that serve them to an
agent host, and where each kind of text lives. The aim is that every rule is written once,
in the one place its kind belongs, so that changing it changes every agent that follows it,
and no two copies drift apart.

## 1. Layers

Crustify is text in three layers, with one more per run:

| layer | where | voice | holds |
|---|---|---|---|
| skills | `skills/<group>/<name>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what Crustify's artifacts are and how its work is done: workflows, how-tos, conventions, schemas |
| tool skills | `skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md` | descriptive, third person | what each tool is, and how it serves each stage |
| agents | `agents/<agent>.md`, with `agents/common.md`, and the assistant's under `agents/assistant/` | instructive, second person | an agent's identity, inputs, what it owns, its steps and what its role changes in the skill index |
| task messages | `task.md` beside a run's `task.json` | instructive | what one run is given: its inputs, and what it needs beyond its role |

Each artifact's schema, the meaning of its fields, is a skill under `skills/artifacts/`,
and an example of each is given under `templates/`, which the schema cites. The settings,
dashboard and `.gitignore` templates there are what a campaign copies to start. Examples
hold illustrations, not rules.

The layers are plain Markdown, so that any agent reads them as files. A provider, under
`providers/<host>/`, serves them to one agent host in its own format, as
[Providers](#4-providers) describes; the layers name no host.

### 1.1 Skills

A skill describes. It states what an artifact holds, how a decision is made, what a
procedure produces and when each of its steps happens, never what an agent should do, and
never who does a step: which agent owns which step is the agents'. It does not name the
tools that serve it either: a skill reads the same whether or not a tool is installed, so
a statement such as "each unit's lifecycle role is established while planning" belongs in
a skill, and the wavefront command that records it belongs in wavefront's tool skill.

Skills are grouped by the part of the work they describe: `workflows/`, `planning/`,
`rust/`, `verification/`, `operations/`, `artifacts/`, `tools/` and `crustify/`. A skill's
name is unique across the groups, since agents invoke it by name. Two kinds of skill
describe how work is done. A how-to, such as `binding` or `porting`, describes how one item
is handled. A workflow, under `workflows/`, describes how one kind of campaign proceeds
from its settings to its results: `setup`, which every campaign shares, and one per kind of
campaign (`binding-workflow`, `porting-workflow`, `audit-workflow`). A workflow names the
how-tos and the layout rather than restating them.

A skill opens with frontmatter that gives its `name` and its `description`. The
description is all an agent sees of the skill before it reads it, so it says what the skill
covers and before which step it is read. A skill stays under about 4,500 tokens, so that a
host that brings an invoked skill back after compacting an agent's context brings it back
whole; one that outgrows that is split at a section that another step needs on its own.
The parts sit in sub-directories of the skill's own, `skills/<group>/<skill>/<part>/SKILL.md`,
each named `<skill>-<part>`, and the skill's own `SKILL.md` keeps what they share: `binding`
and `porting` keep their boundaries, and their `-types` and `-symbols` parts their routes.

A skill's directory may also hold a script the skill describes, with its tests beside it,
standard library only, so that it runs wherever the skill is read: `usage` holds
`crustify-usage`.

A skill or an agent says what a step does and which program does it, never the program's
command lines, flags or options, which change with the program: the program's own `--help`
and documentation give them, and the text sends its reader there. A command appears only
where its exact form is what must hold, and a procedure of several commands that must run
exactly so is a script beside its skill, documented by its own `--help`.

Every skill's sections are numbered. A reference to a section names it, with or without its
number ("testing-builds' Coverage section", "layout § Lifecycle › Waves"), so that a renumbering
never silently points a reference at another section. A skill links another by its
relative path, with the other's name as the link's text.

### 1.2 Agents

An agent instructs. Its file holds what is specific to it: its place among the agents, its
inputs, its workflow steps, and the guidelines that apply to one step or stage. Where a step
follows a skill, the agent names the skill's section rather than restating it ("as the
`scheduling` skill's Order section describes"); where a step adds to it, the agent states
only the addition.

An agent states what it owns by naming the skill sections it carries out ("you create and
purge every level of the `layout` skill's Lifecycle section"), and adds only what the
skills leave to it: the commands it runs, the judgements it makes, the cases it must not
handle itself.

Every agent's prompt opens with `agents/common.md`: that every commit takes the identity
[`versioning`](../../operations/versioning/SKILL.md)'s Identity section gives, that a task
message's instructions take precedence over the rest of the prompt, except where a skill or a
role says a task message adds to a check and never relaxes it, and how skills and
tool skills are read. Every agent sees every skill, with its description:
its host lists them, or, for a host that does not, the provider fills the index of every
skill at common's `<!-- SKILL INDEX -->` marker from the skills' names and descriptions, so
that each description is written once.

The agent's own file follows, in three sections, every agent alike:

- `## Role`: who the agent is, its place among the agents, what it owns and what it leaves
  to others;
- `## Workflow`: its steps, each naming the skills it follows. A skill the description
  already sends the agent to before a step needs no mention; a step names a skill where
  only part of it applies to the agent, or where the agent follows it only in some runs;
  and
- `## Inputs`: what its task message names.

An agent's file names no value of one run: an integration branch or a batch id is "the one
your task message names". `{crustify_root}` stands for the path of Crustify's checkout,
which a provider fills.

The assistant has one file for every kind of campaign, `agents/assistant/assistant.md`, with a
`<!-- CAMPAIGN ROLE -->` marker at the end of its Role and a `<!-- CAMPAIGN WORKFLOW -->`
marker as its Workflow, which take the campaign kind's file,
`agents/assistant/translate.md` for a port or wrap campaign or `agents/assistant/audit.md`
for an audit: its `### Campaign` section, what the assistant owns in that kind of campaign,
and, after its `<!-- WORKFLOW -->` marker, its steps.

### 1.3 Tool skills

A tool is one program an agent reaches for: wavefront, ffimap, ffibox. Each has one skill,
`skills/tools/<tool>/SKILL.md`, written as every skill is, descriptively and without naming
agents. It states what a campaign uses the tool for, where the tool's state sits in a
campaign, and how the tool's output becomes Crustify's artifacts and decisions. How the
tool works, its configuration, tables, commands and what they mean, is its own
documentation's, which the skill cites by document rather than restating, so that the two
never drift; a fact that documentation lacks is added to it, on a branch of the tool's
repository, not to the skill.

A tool skill opens with what the tool is, which documentation of its own is read in full
before its first use, and what holds in every use of it; one section per stage follows,
each subsection named after the skill section it adds to ("Scheduling › Order"), stating
only what the tool adds there and naming the documents of the tool that stage reads. Its
description names the stages and steps it serves.

An agent reads a tool's skill before the first step of its work that the skill's
description names, as `agents/common.md` says, and no other skill names a tool: the
description alone brings an agent to the tool, so it names every stage and step the tool
serves. A tool is removed by deleting its skill.

## 2. Placement

| text | goes in |
|---|---|
| what an artifact's fields mean | its schema skill under `skills/artifacts/` |
| what an artifact looks like | its example under `templates/` |
| how a kind of work is done, independent of tools | the skill for that work |
| how a kind of campaign proceeds, step by step | its workflow skill under `skills/workflows/`, with the steps every campaign shares in `setup` |
| a convention every agent follows | `conventions` |
| what one agent does, in which steps, and which steps it owns | that agent's file under `agents/` |
| what every agent holds | `agents/common.md` |
| what the assistant does in one kind of campaign | `agents/assistant/<kind>.md` |
| what a tool is, and how it serves each stage | its tool skill |
| how one host is served the layers | its provider under `providers/<host>/` |
| what one run needs beyond its role | its task message, `task.md` |
| what Crustify is for, which every change is judged against | `GOALS.md`, at Crustify's root |
| how Crustify repairs and improves itself | [`evolution`](../evolution/SKILL.md) |
| which changes landed, and whether each held | `EVOLUTION.md`, at Crustify's root |
| a rule that holds for one target alone | that campaign's `crustify/LESSONS.md` |

A rule that two agents share goes in a skill both read, not in both agents. A rule that
names a tool goes in the tool's skill. A change to a rule is made where the rule lives;
text that restates it elsewhere is removed rather than kept in step.

## 3. Runs

A stage's agent runs with its file as its system prompt and its task as its first message:
the task message names what its `## Inputs` section lists and the instructions its run
needs beyond its role, if any. Its file is the same for every run of the stage, so that runs at once share their
whole system prompt in the provider's cache. The assistant runs the same way, as the main
agent of a session in a campaign's repository, with its file and its campaign kind's as
its system prompt.

## 4. Providers

A provider serves the layers to one agent host, in that host's format, and holds nothing
the layers do not: every file it carries is generated from them, wires them in, or carries
what its host needs of its own.

The generic provider, `providers/generic/`, composes each agent's prompt for any host:
`compose.py <agent> [<kind>]` prints `agents/common.md`, with the skill index filled, and
the agent's file, the assistant's with its campaign kind's. A host without a provider of
its own takes that prompt as its agent's instructions, and reads each skill's `SKILL.md`
by its path. The other providers compose through it.

The Claude Code provider, `providers/claude/`, makes Crustify's checkout a plugin, whose
manifest is `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`:

- the skills, by their group directories and the directory of each part of a split skill,
  which the manifest lists on its own since Claude Code scans a listed directory one level
  deep, invoked as `crustify:<name>`;
- `agents/`, one plugin agent per stage, `crustify:<stage>`, and one assistant per campaign
  kind, `crustify:assistant-translate` and `crustify:assistant-audit`. A plugin agent's
  body replaces Claude Code's own system prompt, so each body opens with that prompt,
  `system-prompt.md`, followed by the generic provider's prompt without the skill index,
  since Claude Code lists the plugin's skills to every agent. Each agent's
  frontmatter gives the description the assistant routes a run by;
- `system-prompt.md`, Claude Code's own system prompt, captured from a real request by
  `dump-system-prompt.py`, less its one project's `# Memory` section, and dumped again
  when Claude Code is upgraded;
- `spawn.py`, which launches a stage run as a Claude Code process of its own, since Claude
  Code refuses a subagent's writes of report files, and copies its transcript into
  Crustify's home; the assistants' prompts end with how they launch through it;
- `hooks.json`: a `SubagentStop` hook, `transcripts.py`, which copies each stage agent's
  transcript into Crustify's home, for a stage run a host launches as a subagent; and
- `compose.py`, which generates the agents (`compose.py build`).

The generated files are committed, and regenerated whenever `agents/` or
`system-prompt.md` changes.

## 5. Language

Programmers and agents read Crustify's texts and a campaign's, so they are written plainly,
as the [Google developer documentation style guide](https://developers.google.com/style)
describes: one term per thing, short sentences, a condition before its consequence, lists for
parallel items. A rule keeps its reason, since agents generalize from reasons. A rewrite keeps
every fact of the old text, which its review checks. The voice rules of [Layers](#1-layers)
stay: a skill describes, an agent instructs.
